subsubtopic: UNIVERSAL ACCESS TO FAIR ORAL HEARINGS BEFORE REFUGEE BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege and an honour to present a petition pursuant to Standing Order 106 on behalf of a number of western
Canadians who remind the House of Commons that the standing committee of Parliament responsible for immigration regulations has proposed a new procedure for refugees which, if adopted, would fairly and effectively solve the problems of backlogs and all the unsubstantiated claims.
This particular proposal has received widespread support from not only all Parties of Parliament but from the Canadian Council of Churches, the Canadian Bar Association, the Canadian Jewish Congress and actually most other groups or individuals knowledgeable on refugee issues.
Therefore, the petitioners are asking the Government of Canada to withdraw Bill C-55 and substitute it with legislation embodying the principles of fair and quick oral hearings of claims made by refugee claimants, and these ought to be made before a refugee board independent of the Immigration Commission, providing universal access to such hearings for every applicant in Canada. The claimants also ought to have the right to appeal on the basis of fact.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 106 I have a petition from approximately 250 residents of Essex County who are particularly concerned about the operation and further construction of the Fermi II Nuclear Plant on the U.S. side of the border just adjacent to my constituency.
The petitioners come from Amherstburg, Harrow, Sandwich West, Colchester, Malden, Anderdon, and a good many other parts of my constituency. The petitioners are most concerned to see that there is a Canadian presence which plays an equal role with the United States in reviewing the safety of Fermi II before this nuclear reactor is permitted to move any further toward full operation.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and a privilege to present a petition on behalf of people in my riding from the community of Coudouc. Petitioners wish to convey their disagreement with the new corporate plan for Canada Post.

Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome this opportunity today to speak in this historic debate.
When the first ministers met this spring to discuss the conditions set by Quebec for joining the Constitution, not many people really believed that they would be able to reach an agreement. It would take a miracle, people said. The day after the agreement was signed, people said it was a miracle.
Mr. Speaker, 1 have been trained to be sceptical about miracles, and I don't think there has ever been a miracle in politics. I am inclined to believe that the Meech Lake Accord was achieved by one man, our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and that the premiers' readiness to consider the conditions set by Quebec reflect the "maturing" of our Canadian society.
Mr. Speaker, in the course of my speech I intend to focus on the central aspect of the Meech Lake Accord; the recognition in the Constitution of Quebec's distinct character and Canada's linguistic duality. For the first time, the provinces are making a formal commitment to protect this linguistic duality, and Quebec, which from now on will be recognized as a distinct society, will have the recognized right and privilege to protect and promote that which constitutes its specific character.
In the lives of nations there are important events that have become milestones because they have changed the course of history. Madam Speaker, this historic Accord is one of those milestones.
1 would now like to take a few moments to correct a serious mistake I am referring to the theory that the claims of modern day Quebec started in the 1960s, and that the measures taken during those years represent a clean break with the years that went before, the governments Quebec had since the 1930s and the leaders of public opinion who had crafted a nationalist ideology in the years before that time. In fact, nothing could be further from the truth.
The history of nations-the history of Quebec and Canada is a case in point-consists of deep political currents that determine its flow and a number of superficial events that sometimes camouflage, sometimes reveal, the meaning of these currents. Quebec in the 1960s-this turbulent Quebec that is said to be at the root of our Constitutional reform-was not, and never has been, a brand new Quebec come out of the blue in our modern history. It was merely developing what had always been there and what had been expressed formerly in

other ways. Between Quebec politicians like Maurice Duples-sis, who stated: "We must keep what we have", Jean Lesage, who said: "We must be masters in our own house" and Daniel Johnson, who demanded: "Equality or independence", there was never a break. Superficially perhaps, but beneath it all, a steady continuity.
Mr. Speaker, our Francophone society in Canada has been constant in its desire to be recognized as a distinct society, in charge of its own affairs.
Everyone knows that if it were not for the resistance of the Atlantic Provinces, especially Nova Scotia, and if it were not' for the French Canadians in Lower Canada, the union of the colonies of British North America would probably had been legislative, not federative. In fact, as indicated by the central authority's use of the power of disallowance after 1867, attempts were made in that direction during the initial years of Confederation.
These attempts to make the provinces into a uniform body, under the authority of the central Government, as others have often wanted to do, could never succeed in the Canadian context, especially where Quebec was concerned.
To quote Jean-Charles Bonenfant, an eminent professor who also was my professor: "The spirit of 1867 was the final acceptance of the existence of French Canadians and a logical consequence of the Quebec Act". He goes on to say: "The Fathers of Confederation made Lower Canada-the future province of Quebec-a province where the French Canadian majority would be in charge of its own affairs, although it was forced to give the English-speaking minority exceptional protection: Article 93 on education, the twelve privileged townships, the Legislative Council and legislative bilingualism as laid down subsequently Article 133 of the British North America Act."
Madam Speaker, how could it have been otherwise? French Canadians are different because of their language, their laws and their history. Since the Quebec Act was passed in the 18th century, and despite a succession of constitutional reforms and systems, Quebec always had the power to create its own institutions, governed by legislation that has developed an essential part of its social structure and still does today.
One of the main reasons why Quebec is a distinct society arises from this different social structure and a different way of doing things, based on a different system of values and regulated, as far as private law is concerned, by a series of laws that go back to the "coutume de Paris" and are thus not based on the same philosophy as the common law of the other provinces. This applies to all Quebec citizens, whatever their origins or language.
French Canadians have always claimed they had all the elements of a distinct society, and in the course of history, they have managed to give their distinct character a firm foundation which they would now like to see recognized. They did so during the parliamentary struggles in the first half of the 19th
Constitution Amendment, 1987
century, Madam Speaker. They showed their mettle under the Act of Union by gradually introducing what was in fact a double system.
Of course, the strategy has changed over time. As we all know, the State has not always been as strategically important to French Canadians as it was during the first half of the 19th century and still is today. For a long time and, significantly, especially after Confederation, French Canadian leaders made the Catholic school system and the parish the prime instrument for protecting and promoting the French fact in Canada and North America. Unfortunately, among certain representatives, sometimes even the most enlightened, of English Canada, this approach lead to incredible misunderstandings and considerable conflict. In whatever ways Francophones have, over the years, made their claim for recognition as a distinct society, it has always been one of the major currents of Canadian history. Only a blind person would fail to see that.
This is how Quebec's international claims throughout the 1960s-indeed, just like its claims in other fields, communications, to name one-stem primarily from the all exclusive approach taken by previous governments with respect to maintaining their constitutional prerogative. When Paul Gerin-Lajoie stated in 1965 that the Quebec Government could actively participate in an international conference of education ministers, thus exercising his power in an exclusive constitutional jurisdiction, he was in fact doing nothing more than drawing implicit conclusions flowing from the stated position to which Premier Duplessis and his predecessors had been clinging all along. There was nothing new under the sun.
Madam Speaker, why did the undertaking turn out to be so arduous? Why so many obstacles on such a straight road? Why did the staunchest opposition come from the Canadian Government until 1984? Why are the same people again today so adamantly opposed to official recognition of the distinct character of the Quebec society?
Nobody denies the existence of the patently obvious distinctive characteristics of Quebec: 80 per cent of the people speak French. It is the only government in America where Francophones make up the majority. Montreal happens to be Canada's French-speaking cultural community, to the extent that the vitality of our country's Francophone minorities depends on the vitality of Quebec's society. Madam Speaker, the most eloquent testimony to Quebec's distinct character is the deep-rooted link with its electronic media, as emphasized by the Sauvageau-Caplan task force on broadcasting policies: high local ratings, preference for original dramatic productions, and what have you.
So, Madam Speaker, why should anyone speak out against constitutional recognition of Quebec's distinct character? Why does opposition to that still prevail today?

Just as history is made up of deep-rooted trends and passing events, so do we have both sincere and superficial politicians. Except for a very short interregnum in 1979, from 1966 to 1984-almost 20 years-Canada was inspired and directed by politicians who remained insensitive to these deep-rooted trends and were more interested in imposing the abstact formula of a country which they did not understand, or at least did not seem to understand properly.
This country, obviously, is made up of strong regions which want to maintain their own characteristics. It is home to two linguistic communities. It includes a Francophone society whose mainstay is and has always been Quebec, the only government where it makes up the majority. That is Canada as it is, Madam Speaker, not an abstract but a real entity.
The policy of confrontation which we had to put up with through all those years could only lead to the situation we all witnessed: absolutely untractable positions and a separatist threat which was all the more astonishing that it did originate from Quebec's need to take its normal place within Confederation, nothing more than its normal place.
I would not want to suggest that all demands made by Quebec were not to be interpreted, therefore negotiable. I am simply saying that they all stemmed from Quebecers' will to assert themselves, and as such it was not in any way a challenge to the sovereignty nor, of course, the very existence of Canada. Nothing suggests, except in the stubborn minds of a few men who finally managed to impose to most people, Quebecers and other Canadians alike, the somewhat perverse notion that the qualifier "Canadian" quite simply excluded the qualifier "Quebecer", that being Canadian meant being against Quebec, with the all too natural consequence that such a tenet would soon be inversely expressed by Quebecers themselves.
Inevitably, this refusal by the Government in Ottawa to recognize Quebec's distinct character was to provoke a similar reaction from the other side. It was not a happy episode in our history.
However, nothing could be further from the basic reality of this country, especially for the Francophone community. To quote our Prime Minister in his famous speech in Sept-iles, where he promised to bring Quebec back into the Canadian Constitution:
Quebecers love Quebec and are proud of Canada. They also love Canada
and are proud of Quebec. Their hearts are big enough for both loyalties. Very
few people who said yes to Quebec said no to Canada, and no one who said yes
to Canada said no to Quebec.
That is the Canadian situation, Madam Speaker.
This double allegiance, which many foreigners have trouble understanding, was pledged by all great French Canadian nationalists, ever since Confederation. Lavergne, Asselin, Bourassa- incidently, Henri Bourassa was a typical example: He was a man who was truly French Canadian, who clearly defined the French Canadian fact, and who at the same time was every inch a Canadian. At a time when Canada was the
victim of imperialist and extraterritorial intervention, he defended Canada's autonomy against intervention by foreign powers, including Great Britain. This position, taken by a man of vision, would be vindicated several years later when the Treaty of Westminster was signed.
Fortunately, Madam Speaker, in 1984 Canadians and Quebecers elected a man cut from the right cloth, who understood that the very nature of the Canadian federation demanded the intelligent art of compromise, co-operation and standing united for a common goal. For almost 20 years,-we all witnessed this period in our history- Ottawa's stubborn insistence on making Quebec knuckle under, for the sake of an egalitarian vision of this country, nearly broke up both Quebec and Canada. In hardly three years, the patience and intelligence of one man made it possible to restore the common will of all Canadians which has always been, and still is, the strength of our federation.
We can thank the Prime Minister for Meech Lake. For the first time, Quebec sees enshrined in the Constitution its right to protect and promote that which constitutes its distinct character, and it will be able to evoke this distinct identity in all disputes about fundamental rights in the Charter.
Another significant gain is the long hoped for recognition of Canada's linguistic duality, and even more important, a commitment by each province to protect that duality. Madam Speaker, for the first time in Canada's history, each province is constitutionally committed to protect the French language. As was said by Mr. Decary when he testified before the joint committee, it is a major gain for Francophones outside Quebec, both morally and in its practical impact. From now on, the Constitution, the Charter and all language and education rights shall be interpreted so as to guarantee the protection of the French-speaking community. That is a reality. That is a victory for Canada and Canadians, Madam Speaker.
Some critics of the Meech Lake Accord have said that one of the most important achievements of the Constitution Act, 1982, in other words, the rights contained in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, might be jeopardized as a result of the recognition of Quebec's distinct character. Madam Speaker, here again, the Meech Lake Accord is merely proposing a new balance between individual and collective rights. As mentioned time and time again by our Prime Minister, none of the rights in the Charter will be superseded or quashed as a result of Quebec being recognized as a distinct society. In fact, up to now, the interpretation of fundamental rights given by the courts have always been based on sociological realities, including Quebec's distinct character. The Meech Lake Accord will simply state unequivocally what has been so far implicitly recognized.
As a matter of fact so far, any attempt at making Canada a unitary country has failed and if, by its very nature, this country has been strong it is only because of the strength and vitality of its various parts. Madam Speaker, there lie the basic
October 19, 1987

differences between the Canadian and American federations going in opposite directions. The Canadian federation, which was highly centralized at the beginning, had to struggle until it found a proper balance between its component parts through a decentralization process. On the other hand, the American federation which was very decentralized followed the road towards centralization. The Meech Lake Accord, as we are all well aware, reflects this deep-rooted process. We have restored each component of the Canadian society to its proper place. Above all, we have finally given Quebec its proper place; all we had to do was to forget this depressing period of our history when confrontation ruled supreme, to simply open the door, ask all interested parties to get together and give Quebecers and other Canadians something they had every right to expect, namely a country, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, everyone in the House recognizes that this is a special kind of debate, one that is not within the normal range of quick, 30-second flashes and repartee in Parliament. We are talking about something which goes to the fundamental heart of the country. It requires from each and every Member on both sides of the House a sense of judgment on what is the best way in which they can serve the interests of their constituents, both in a local sense and in a national sense.
My starting point in trying to address the issue is a recognition of how important federalism is to Canada. Probably of all countries in the world, certainly all those with so-called federal arrangements, federalism is most important to us.
A little joke has been used many times about a question being posed to a Russian, an American, and a Canadian, asking them to define sex. The Russian says: "It is a capitalist conspiracy". The American says: "Sex is simply a natural evolution of liberty and the pursuit of happiness". The Canadian says: "It is a federal-provincial problem". This probably reflects what most Canadians innately understand, that our constitutional, legal, institutional framework setting up the powers between Governments and the way we relate to each other is in fact crucial because Canada could not operate without a federal system.
In a sense our geography is a series of connecting settlements across 5,000 kilometres. A sense of distribution at different levels of Government is required to manage it properly. The fundamental issue of French-English relations as they have evolved over the years also requires a federal system to maintain a dynamic between the two. Certainly the relationship, that is, the connection between an economically and politically strong, powerful central Canada and the peripheries, or the hinterlands of East and West, requires a federal system to adjust it, to monitor it, and to keep it alive and dynamic.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
The most difficult relationship in some ways is that of trying to continue to occupy the northern half of the continent when our neighbour is the most powerful nation in the world, and of trying to maintain our independence, uniqueness, and distinctiveness in that relationship. This has also required a federal system to ensure that we could undertake the kind of social experimentation and the variations in developing that distinctive notion of what is Canada.
Today we find that we have a convergence of all those problems. In a sense, debating the Meech Lake Accord and the Langevin agreement is only one part of the great Canadian debate which seems to be taking place on what is our national purpose and how we answer those issues which have seized Canada since its inception, not only in terms of French-English relations but in terms of central Canada's relationship with the peripheries and its relationship with the United States.
Many of us see quite a fundamental alteration taking place in those relationships. It is a fundamental alteration because on virtually every front we now have a Government in Ottawa which basically does not believe in using Government to serve those purposes. It may see Government as an arbitrator, a mediator or perhaps a conciliator, but not as an initiator, a leader or a driving, motivating force to provide some sense of national purpose or direction in dealing with each of the issues. It comes as no surprise; it is not unique.
Canadian history has been replete with a very strong debate, or conflict at times, between two groups of thought or two competing notions of how Canada should operate, that between the community of communities we are simply an amalgam of separate islands somehow related in an archipelago of convenience, versus those who see Canada as something that the sum of which is greater than its parts. This group of thought indicates that the country of Canada has a unique destiny and responsibility of its own which is larger, bigger, more important, and more significant than the sum of its parts. This is the classic debate in which we have all been engaged.
The problem is that that reality is not in any way encompassed by the Meech Lake Accord, the document which was signed by the Premiers and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) several months ago. If I have any real objection-and I know some of my colleagues feel the same-it is that so much of the new reality of the distinctive Canada about which I was talking is not incorporated in the agreement.
If we read the testimony presented by women's organizations before the standing committee, we see that they basically said that the Meech Lake Accord does not incorporate the new reality of women in our society and in our economy, that it does not grant them the kind of recognition of the rights for which they have fought so long. It does not take into account the kinds of concerns which my colleague from New Brunswick and I have in our constituencies about French-speaking

Constitution Amendment, 1987
Canadians outside the Province of Quebec. It is not incorporated in the Meech Lake Accord; it does not recognize those problems.
The Accord does not take into account the incredibly new sense of western direction, enthusiasm, and energy, to be more in control and managing our own resources. We do not see anywhere a recognition by the negotiators of the agreement of a demand for some accommodation on the part of the central provinces to greater representation at the national level. There is a fundamental flaw made in the country in assuming that provincial Governments will represent regional interests nationally. We are almost trying to devise a new kind of institution called federal-provincial conferences to make that kind of regional representation work.
However, we know that the founders of Confederation made a mistake, one which no successive generations corrected. The Upper Chamber was originally designed to ensure that there would be a sense of region at the national level of government, which was totally and completely destroyed by the fact that it was an appointed body. Because no one got around to changing it has meant that our federalism has always had a real flaw. It has not ensured an effective representation of the interests of western Canada and Atlantic Canada at the national level.
The movement toward that achievement was at a point of maturity, when the opportunity for major constitutional change to have an elected Senate based on some form of equal representation was about ready to blossom forward, but the Meech Lake Accord was signed to cut that off. That accommodation is more difficult now because the Accord establishes the principles of unanimity to make that kind of constitutional change.
In a sense our institutional document is further out of sync with the living reality of Canada itself. It is what political scientists call the living constitution, that kind of amalgam of political, social and economic forces that shift and change from generation to generation but which must give life to our Constitution.
Certainly the Meech Lake Accord does not take into account that since the Second World War there has emerged in Canada a new generation of Canadians, the so-called multicultural third force of Canada, which in some ways is the most dynamic part of our country. They find the Meech Lake Accord frustrates and freezes their ambitions and their aspirations. That is why there has been so much consternation, certainly in our Party and among many other Canadians.
This kind of constitutional initiative serves one very vital and important purpose, to have the Province of Quebec as a signatory, a purpose for which our own Party has fought. In our own policy resolution I spoke on behalf of western Canadians to encourage the convention to join in that ambition, but that noble and very positive achievement has been
substantially marred by the other part of the equation which was given in order to achieve that goal.
We have taken certain steps backward. We have been blind to those new realities and we have created a very flawed and imperfect document. In fact, it may have put at some risk the effective evolution of Canada because we have put roadblocks or apparent barriers in the way.
I was reading a book by Donald Smiley called The Federal Condition In Canada. I think most people recognize that Professor Smiley is one of the foremost constitutional experts in Canada. Talking about the sense of national purpose and national policy, he said that there have been three real periods. First, John A. Macdonald in the 1870s had a national policy, which seemed to capture a sense of a broader Canada. Second, the period after the Second World War when we got together to forge a new set of social and economic institutions: the health care system, the regional equalization system and so on. Third, in the early 1980s the Government of which I was a member in its constitutional change attempted a kind of national resource policy. Professor Smiley ended with his comment:
-if John A. Macdonald were to reappear among us, he would within a
month have a surer grasp of the stakes in our current debates than does the
person who is now the Prime Minister.
The first Conservative Prime Minister of Canada, John A. Macdonald, would have understood that, aside from simply accommodating regional, linguistic or ethnic interests, a broader sense of vision and purpose is also required. The present Accord fails on that account miserably. It ends up with a scuffling of private interests as a definition of what Canada is all about.
That is why the amendments put forward by members of our Party are so important and essential for consideration by this House. They are not in any way to impair the achievement of the Meech Lake Accord, which is the involvement of Quebec in the constitutional structure, but to say that it could be a much better, much improved document accommodating a much more realistic contemporary sense of what Canada is and what Canada should be. The amendments are simply to say, let us alter and reorganize to achieve a constitutional legal framework which better represents the interests of all Canadians and the reality of Canada. Those amendments are not in any way reducing the achievement. They add and support it. In particular they are trying to say to Members of this House that in no way would damage be done.
We are now locked into a kind of struggle reminiscent of certain Japanese wrestlers, those 400 pound behemoths who get into the centre ring, grasp each other and are afraid to move. It seems we almost have that now with the federal and provincial Governments. They have locked each other into a death grip and each one is afraid to move even though they know that there probably is a necessity for change and amendment.

I would say in parenthesis that perhaps there is some movement, at least on the provincial side. It may appear that there are certain provincial Governments which are now saying that their work was incomplete and not good enough. They must take into account the questions of how they respond to challenges to the Charter, the rights of the Territories and how they deal with the rights of the aboriginal peoples, the new realities of the Canada with which we are dealing.
We on this side of the House can only say Amen to those kinds of efforts because we know that change will have to be made. We also know that there is a smaller reality, namely, that this House will be required to vote in a matter of days or a week on the specific interest.
It is of great and incredible regret that the Prime Minister of Canada, the one person responsible for trying to have a broader vision, was not prepared to use those skills of conciliation, that he is so proud of boasting about, to deal with the kind of representations made in front of the standing committee. He instead stonewalled every opportunity for change, which flew in the face of valid important representations for change.
That, therefore, puts this House of Commons in an awkward dilemma. Because of the unwillingness and impolitic behaviour of the Government, the House of Commons is in a very difficult situation which we all realize. Everyone supports the ambition of Quebec to gain its sense of distinction and place in the Canadian Constitution, but to do that we must agree to an Accord which we also know does not recognize fully the rights and interests of many other Canadians or their concerns. That is the $64 question which colleagues on both sides of the House must face.
I suggest purely on my own account that ultimately we have to come to a choice based upon how to achieve the most effective kinds of constitutional changes for Canada, that will allow us to pursue a country that is modern, contemporary and recognizes its many changes over time. My conclusion is that we will not do it with this Government. It will be impossible to achieve with the kinds of initiatives that we have seen. For example, the kind of wrenching alteration in the fundamental structures of Canada that will be occasioned if the free trade agreement goes through. There is the total uprooting and dismantling of the federal Government's ability to provide direction and leadership on regional development, on social programs and economic development, and, in fact, in meeting international competition because we will no longer have a Government which has the power or strength to provide that leadership. We will have signed it away. We will have constricted our abilities and eliminated our capacity to develop programs to take initiative. It is a further sign that this group of people does not understand that government itself in its own right is a positive, creative, constructive force which must be used for those purposes. They have decided that the great allocator of the Canadian national interest will be the marketplace and that the Government is only there to facilitate that

as opposed to providing a public interest, not a private interest, a public interest.
What's wrong with that?

Even the Hon. Member from Mississauga does not understand the difference between public and private interest, that the Government is not simply there to reflect a whole series of private, profit-oriented interests. When people vote for a Member of Parliament they expect him to serve the public interest, and that public interest is bigger and broader than the whole series of individualized, selfish private interests.
Every Government has to accommodate business and labour and everything else, but it should not surrender to them or become captive to them. It should have a broader set of interests than that which is something that the Conservatives of the 1980s do not understand. They have no sense of that kind of public interest. We see it in the individual behavior of Members and ir, the behavior of the Government. That is why it is so essential, when looking at constitutional structures and institutions, we assure that the sense of public, national purpose is redefined and that we have a Government that understands that, for a change, and will bring those kinds of concerns to bear.
Ultimately, we will fight as hard as we can and for as long as we have a breath left for these amendments. If they are defeated, as the Prime Minister says they will be, then we will need a Government beyond this one which will pursue those same amendments in the same way to ensure that we will have a Constitution that fully recognizes and reflects the reality of Canada. My job will be to ensure that there is the basis for that alternative Government so that we can have an effective and useful Canada with an effective Government that recognizes those concerns. That will be the kind of decision which I will urge my colleagues to take as well.

I came to Canada as a youngster with my family in the early 1950s. We were fleeing the wars that had ravaged Europe and Southeast Asia. To be able to stand here and participate in a debate over the Constitution of this country is for me personally a very important and moving moment. That I can do so says

much about what Canada is. Surely there are very few countries in this world where a newcomer can be elected and participate, as I am doing now, in debating the constitution form of that country. It says something about this country and its broadness of vision that an immigrant can be elected to this place. I am not the only one; there are many others in this House who were born in countries other than Canada. It says a lot about Canada that this opportunity exists for newcomers.
The fact that we are standing here debating the Constitution also says something about Canada. It indicates what a young country we are. We are attempting to define our essence. Surely that is what a Constitution is all about.
This process started in 1982. 1 had hoped then to have an opportunity to participate in the debate on the Constitution Act of 1982. Unfortunately I did not have the opportunity. Some of the things I want to say today are things I had wanted to say in that debate.
At that time I was disturbed when the former Liberal Government under Mr. Trudeau brought in that legislation because there were several aspects which I did not think were correct. First, I thought it was a power grab by the central Government. The federal Government was attempting to act unilaterally to change the nature and shape of this country in a dramatic fashion. It was not until the Supreme Court came down with quite a historic decision that the Prime Minister realized he had better start talking to the provinces to get their understanding and agreement. That is what happened; compromises were reached and we ended up with the Constitution Act of 1982.
It is interesting to note that the process by which we reached that agreement was one of consultation, wheeling and dealing, discussions, and compromises among the elected Governments of this country. That also says so much about what Canada really is. The federal Government's move in 1981-82 disturbed that balance.
I was also disturbed because the original document Mr. Trudeau introduced would have increased the powers of the federal Government. I for one have always believed that the nature of Canada is reflected in the division of powers between the federal and provincial Governments. I have been a strong believer in the notion of co-operative federalism. To govern a country as diverse as Canada, with its various regional interests, linguistic and economic groups, is best done through a co-operative, flexible, compromising kind of system.
That leads me to my second area of concern about what Mr. Trudeau started in 1982. That was his attempt to cast our Constitution in stone. I believe that to be a major problem still. He attempted to define in legalistic terms where the power should be, what our rights are, and what are the roles of the various Governments. We are living in an age of very rapid technological, social, psychological and cultural change. I believe our Constitution should have remained flexible. What we had was a collection of different Acts and documents, some of them going back to Westminster, the BNA Act, and

October 19, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
common law. That was our Constitution. It was not neat, it was not defined in one legalistic document. There were many documents. The Constitution was part of the British heritage of common law as well. It was flexible and open. I believe it would have served Canada much better in the years to come to have maintained a flexible Constitution which would have allowed organic growth and changes as we went into the 21st century and beyond. Casting it in stone by passing specific Bills like the Constitution Act of 1982 has created a rigidity which, I believe, will not serve us in the years ahead. I believe that the co-operative, flexible, organic approach of the past would have served us much better in the future than what we have now.
That leads me to my third concern about the Constitution Act of 1982, that being the areas which were left out. If we were going to begin to define the rights and responsibilities of individuals and various elected bodies, we should have continued. What Mr. Trudeau talked about was really 19th century Liberal ideals. I am not saying that they are necessarily outdated. Individual personal freedoms and rights are important. The document which we have today is still flawed because of its basic omissions, and I will return to that later.
What was missing, in my opinion, was a futuristic outlook. I would have felt much more comfortable and been much more excited had the document talked about some of the issues and concerns which the people of our country will be facing as we approach the 21st century and beyond. The newer technologies of mass communication will create a power for persuasion and propaganda against which I believe the citizens of our country must be protected in the future. That was missing.
I think of the tremendous growth of pollutants in the world today. Our air, water, and soil are being polluted to an ever-increasing extent. There should have been something in the Constitution guaranteeing the right to fresh air and clean water. It would have been admirable to put such rights into our Constitution to ensure that one generation cannot befoul the earth, the air, and the waters for the generations to come.
I am concerned about the erosion which I see of basic social programs such as medicare. We should have included in the Constitution the right to the best medical treatment for all Canadians. That was not included. A country as rich and bountiful in resources as is ours should have included in its Constitution the right to decent housing and to food on the table. Canadians living in this beautiful and bountiful nation should inherit the right to decent housing and food on the table.
All of those things were missing from the 1982 Constitution Act. In many ways the Constitution Act was a 19th century Liberal document and I think we should have had a 21st century document.
Those were my concerns about Mr. Trudeau's constitution. The Meech Lake Accord is some steps further down the road
on which Mr. Trudeau started us. I congratulate the Premiers and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on their accomplishment in devising an agreement which includes Quebec, the sister culture, in the Constitution. That was an important achievement. It would have been very difficult for Canadians to have continued to live with a Constitution which Quebec had not signed. That would have helped to create and foster alienation in the future.
However, there are things in the agreement which must trouble us all. For example, with regard to the definition of a separate society, our common sense tells us that the culture and psychology in Quebec is different. We rejoice in the difference because it strengthens Canada. In fact, it was the French culture in Quebec which helped protect Canada from the persuasive influence and power of the United States. Quebec is very important in ensuring that Canada maintains its sense of identity. Without Quebec, English Canada would have become much more Americanized. Quebec reminds us that we are indeed different and that is very important.
However, to define that in legalistic terms is very difficult, if not impossible. That is why it is difficult to have a Constitution which requires a definition for everything, which requires the casting in stone of every aspect of this country. It is an impossible task which entangles us in a legal jungle into which our Constitution is leading us further.
There are things about the Meech Lake Accord that bother me. Many Members on all sides of the House have expressed those concerns. It is wrong that the Yukon and the Northwest Territories will not be allowed to become provinces until all the other provinces agree. That outrages our sense of fairness and justice.
The rights of our aboriginal people is a question yet to be resolved. The country must come to terms with our aboriginal people, our founding fathers-
And mothers.

And mothers. To allow this to remain unresolved is as unacceptable as is keeping Quebec out of the Constitution. It must be a priority of this Parliament and all Parliaments to resolve to bring our aboriginal people into the constitutional family.
The override on women's rights is totally unacceptable. It is incredible that in this day and age there is no guarantee that there shall be no discrimination based on gender. There is an override as well on the issue of minority rights. It is totally unacceptable that people can be discriminated against based on the colour of their skin. That issue must also be resolved.
I am concerned about the reform of the Senate. While I agree with the actions of our Senators in holding up certain Bills-because I disagree with the substance of those Bills as well-I cannot accept the fact that unelected people can stop the work of this House. It is unacceptable that entering into the 21st century we are still saddled with an institution left
October 19, 1987

over from centuries ago. I am afraid that the proposal from the Meech Lake Accord will make the bad situation even worse. I doubt very much that we will have genuine Senate reform. The only change is that federal patronage has become provincial patronage and all 10 provinces will have to agree to give up their powers of patronage. Good luck. I am afraid that will never happen.
Another area of concern which has been eloquently expressed is the concern about social programs. Are we giving with the Meech Lake Accord too much power to the provinces? I was opposed to Mr. Trudeau's initiative because I' thought he took all the power for the federal Government and it seemed to me that social progress in this country has, on the main, occurred at a provincial level. We have had CCF Governments which have introduced things like hospital insurance and medicare, pioneering new social forms which then became popularized and spread throughout the country. Then the federal Government picked them up and established them as national programs.
Very often it is much easier for those of us who are concerned and interested in social progress to try it first on a provincial level. Social programs are very difficult to implement first on a national level because the federal Government is generally concerned with regional, linguistic and cultural differences. It does not have the support of the electorate of provinces that are a little more homogenized. It is easier to get a provincial electorate behind a certain social program, as we did in Saskatchewan in the early 1960s in terms of medicare. To have brought in medicare without first having it established through the provinces I believe would have been impossible.
Medicare first was initiated through the provinces because of the work done by people like T.C. Douglas and Woodrow Lloyd. Woodrow Lloyd was a man I worked with and for, a man I very deeply respected. The role he played in introducing medicare to this country was heroic. Medicare came in through the provinces. That is where the social experiments occur. That is where the social laboratories exit. I think we must make certain that the provinces have the opportunity of performing the social experimentation.
Certainly, what the Liberals originally introduced in the 1982 Constitution Act would have severely prevented this social experimentation from occurring. It was a power grab by that federal Government. My vision of this country is one of co-operative federalism where both levels of government have an important and vital role to play. It is not a case of the federal Government being more important, or the provincial government. They have different roles to play, but fit together to help shape this country into a strong, vibrant, progressive and growing country. To tilt the power in favour of the federal Government or in favour of the provinces does a disservice to how we operate in this country.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
I do not accept the criticism of the Meech Lake Accord that it will stop social progress. It could very well help to engender social programs and allow more social progress to occur by allowing social experimentation in the provinces. It is true that we have in Saskatchewan right now a regressive government where some of the social progress is now being disassembled. I think the federal Government has an important role to play in ensuring that national standards are maintained.
I have stood in my place and asked that the Government curtail funding to the Province of Saskatchewan because of what it is doing with legal aid. The national standards in terms of legal aid are not being met by the Province of Saskatchewan and the federal Government should use the power of the purse. Power should remain with the federal Government. It should not be tilted in favour of one or the other.
I feel that while there are major problems with the Meech Lake Accord because there are things left undone which should be done and the constitutional process is, therefore, not finished, we have taken a few more steps down the road on which Mr. Trudeau sent us. I never liked the road he chose, but once we are on that road we cannot stop. There are many more steps which need to be taken with the Meech Lake Accord. I welcome the recommendation of the standing committee that there be a permanent, standing committee of this House to deal with constitutional amendments. I dearly hope that much of what I said will be wrong, that the Constitution which is evolving will be flexible enough to meet the tremendous challenges of the 21st Century. That is my sincerest wish.

Madam Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his remarks. I always listen to him carefully when he speaks in this House. However, I was quite astonished today by some of his remarks and I would like to put a few questions to him.
First, the Hon. Member referred to 1982 as a power grab by the federal Government. He referred to the original proposal which he then distinguished from the final proposal. I would like him to name one single power, either in the original proposal or in the final proposal, which the federal Government assumed, one single power the federal Government proposed to have transferred from the legislative authority of the provinces to the federal Government. I may be wrong, but I do not recall that initiative making any such proposal.
Second, the Hon. Member was concerned that the 1981 or 1982 proposal made our Constitution more rigid. He said the Constitution should have remained flexible. I do not quite understand what he is driving at there because I see, for example, the procedure for amending the Constitution of Canada, the general procedure under Article 38, which provides a formula to amend the Constitution with the agreement of the Parliament of Canada and two-thirds of the provinces which have 50 per cent of the population. This, to me, is a much more flexible proposal than the constitutional convention we have been operating under for some 45 or 50

October 19, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
years which requires the agreement of all the provinces and the federal Government.
I thought the Hon. Member perhaps opposed the idea of a Charter of Rights but he did say he thought the Charter was important. I would remind him when he talks about the need to address the question of newer technologies or the right to a cleaner environment, the Charter does that in an organic fashion, in a fashion that will grow and can be built upon over the years, namely, Article 7 of the Charter, which refers to every person's right to life, liberty and security of the person. Although that provision may have up to now been somewhat restrictively interpreted by the courts, I think there is the possibility that the provision, with perhaps a broader interpretation over a period of time, could grow into the kind of concept which the Hon. Member says he favours.

Madam Speaker, 1 did take notes and I do have some notations so I think I can answer the Hon. Member's questions. First, he wanted to know what sort of power grab the federal Government attempted to commit in 1981-1982 with the 1982 Constitution Act. First, it acted unilaterally when the Prime Minister attempted to just pass the legislation through the House of Commons and the Senate, and that was it. That in itself was, 1 think, a power grab. As well, there were aspects in the Constitution that certainly disturbed us, for example, guaranteeing interprovincial trade, so that one province could not discriminate against, let us say, companies coming from outside of Canada. We in Saskatchewan felt that provision could have prevented medicare from being introduced in 1961-62 because the provincial public monopoly on medical insurance would have prevented outside insurance companies from operating in Saskatchewan.
In the same way, we felt in Saskatchewan that the same provision would have prevented us from introducing the Saskatchewan Government's automobile insurance because it created a public monopoly, so would have discriminated against outside insurance companies from doing business in Saskatchewan.
Those were some of the concerns we had about the proposals that were introduced by the former Liberal Government. There was no doubt about it, and I think everybody will recognize, that it was a power grab by the central state. The former Prime Minister's disdain for the provinces and provinicial leaders and Premiers was quite widely known. 1 suspect that the only person he really respected was Allan Blakeney because Allan Blakeney was able to stand toe to toe with him on issue after issue.
Unlike his own Cabinet.

The Hon. Member's second question concerned rigidity. Much of what I have said today is that I find going down the road of a written Constitution creates a rigidity. I still believe that. He suggested that the amending formula, after the Constitution Accord of 1982, created more
flexibility than had existed before. He described it as what "seemed" to exist in the previous Constitution. Of course, I appreciate him saying "seemed". The Constitution we had before was a collection of many different documents. It was not defined. It was not focused. It was not totally described in legalistic terms.
Mr. Trudeau, after all, was a great lawyer. He thought in legalistic terms, and reality had to be defined in legalistic terms. For Mr. Trudeau if the Constitution was not defined in legalistic terms, it did not have a reality to it. I was suggesting that perhaps had Mr. Trudeau been more of a poet and less of a technocrat lawyer he could have had the spirit and the essence of this country. He could have realized that the spirit was alive even though it was not defined in legalistic jargon and terms.
Had Mr. Trudeau been more of a poet, we could have had a Constitution that had some poetry in it rather than having it read like the Income Tax Act, dry and dull, something from which only legal scholars can get any inspiration.
The third point that my colleague from the Liberal Party mentioned was the Charter of Rights. He suggested that such collective rights as the environment can be built on in Article 7. I suppose that is true. I suppose some of the objections that he has had toward the Meech Lake Accord can also be built on in Article 7. His logic here escapes me.
The way things stand now, one can build on what is there. Surely, a great deal more building has to be done in terms of women's rights, aboriginal people and so forth. I do not disagree with him that building has to be done.
But I am just saying it was a pity that in 1982 the vision was not great enough to encompass the 21st century; that, in essence, Mr. Trudeau's document was backward looking and not a forward looking. Had it been a forward looking document he would have included the right to fresh air and clean water, the right to a decent basic standard of living, the right to basic minimal medical care in this country, basic rights that Canadians should enjoy from here on in.

As some of my colleagues have done so far, Madam Speaker, I will deal with the Meech Lake Accord which, I think reflects a vision of tolerance as a characteristic feature of Canada in the respect and promotion of its very creative differences.
Having had the privilege to sit last summer on the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on the Meech Lake Accord, I realized, after a few meetings, that I was taking part in an event of major historical significance. And facing the Canadian coats of arms inscribed with the a mari usque ad mare motto, I realized, for the first time in 20 years, the full significance of this symbol.
As so many other Quebecers, following the Meech Lake Constitutional Accord, I felt for the first time really Canadian,
October 19, 1987

while still feeling like a Quebecer. Thanks to the fantastic results achieved by the Premiers and the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), thanks to their faith in the Canadian federation, thanks to their will to be the builders of Canada rather than small-time politicians who care only for political concepts which inevitably change according to the mood of the time and public opinion, for the first time, I realized the meaning of the Canadian motto A mari usque ad mare, from sea to sea, and I felt a bit more confident of my identity as a Canadian, and as a Canadian from Quebec, I wanted to play my part in the Canadian federation.
1 felt better able to identify with this country because I saw that the whole federation was willing to respect my identity and my differences, and I am not speaking about superiority because we are not better than anyone else. The Canadian mosaic reflects these collective differences, which include my own creative differences and my role in this great country. For the first time, I felt that the other communities in Canada, especially the English-speaking community, recognized me, all Quebecers and all French-Canadians as first-class Canadians and as part of this country.
During the hearings of the Joint Committee chaired by Senator Arthur Tremblay and his colleague Chris Speyer, we looked together at all the options offered by this Accord. We looked at what could be fundamental mistakes or weaknesses in the Accord. We heard hundreds of witnesses and dozens of groups who came to express their views on this historic and, according to some people, near miraculous, Constitutional Accord.
I do not know whether some of them acted in good faith or not, but they used what I would call a somewhat fallacious method, and this is unfortunately the trap in which some of our Liberal colleagues in this House have fallen.
Most of them were ecstatic and full of admiration when they saw the beautiful forest we were planting, but immediately after, they got out their axes and began to destroy systematically this historic Accord. Under what pretext? In most cases, because this Accord, as it was made by man, is by definition not perfect. No one on the committee said it was a perfect Accord. However, everyone, including most of our experts, agreed that although the Accord was not perfect, it was an absolutely essential component of the Canadian structure we were building together, and that later on, if need be, we could look at this structure again and make further changes.
In politics like anywhere else, it is much easier to create panic than to create hope, solidarity and unity. It is so much easier to try and scare people. It is so much easier to claim that rights are in jeopardy. For instance, the women of Quebec reminded Canadian women that they could stand on their own two feet and were perfectly able to promote and protect their fundamental rights, rights for which the women of Quebec,
Constitution Amendment, 1987
like many other Canadian women, have fought vigorously and have now won fundamental recognition.
Granted, the Accord does not recognize, does not pay enough attention to and does not define aboriginal rights as such. It is clear that the aboriginal community, despite continuing attempts, has yet to find its true place, and with force and determination, gain recognition for that place within the Constitution. This could not be done. The Accord does not deal with this specifically. The same applies to the Senate.
Western Canada is very much concerned about Senate reform. As a Quebecer, I must say, and I think most of my colleagues will agree, that the issue of Senate reform is not one of our priorities. We don't lose any sleep over it. I think a proposal to abolish the Senate would easily meet with the unanimous or nearly unanimous support of Quebecers. But that was not the purpose of the nation-building exercise in which the Premiers participated.
There were other issues as well that were brought to our attention during these hearings. There was the whole issue of Francophones outside Quebec. Of course we would have preferred to have the Accord both protect and promote their rights, and we said so in Item 14 of our report, namely that the Constitution should provide that all Governments have a duty not only to protect but also to promote Canada's linguistic duality. However, we realized that in the circumstances and for the time being, it would be impossible to win the acceptance of the entire Canadian community. We did not get the impression, and this was later confirmed by others, that some of the Premiers would not agree to both protect and promote the Canadian linguistic duality in their respective provinces.
There was of course criticism of the distinct society concept.
Some people almost jokingly asked: Does it mean something, or does it mean nothing? If it does not mean anything, why is it there? Reference was made to Quebec's society as being a sociological reality which some people simply would not want to see enshrined in a constitutional statute.
I, for one, state that the distinct society concept does not give Quebec any additional power, either in theory or in practice. The issue of division of powers among the central government and the provinces was not raised. But we happen to know that this concept of distinct society really means something. It will undoubtedly enable Quebec's society to expand as much as possible within its jurisdiction, within its own particular fields.
I can only smile when I hear certain people voice fear and concern about recognizing such a society. They say: You will be granting new powers, creating two societies in Canada, two classes of citizens, some who will get preferential treatment and other Canadian men and women of different ethnic origins who will not be in a position to benefit fully. That suggestion is quite wrong.
We must appreciate the fact that these claims were and are still rooted in Quebec history. One has to bear in mind that

October 19, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
francophone Canadians and Quebecers in particular constitute a small society surrounded on all sides by 350 million Englishspeaking people. My God, this is the way, not to defend our interests to the detriment of anybody else, but to promote our own distinct character if we want to survive.
The assimilation figures for the other provinces and for Canada in general are such that it is obvious that if we are not given the means to remain what we are as a society, we shall not be able to resist for long. Our society is an asset for Canada. It is part of the essence of this country, and what I want myself is to be part of the essence of this country, but for that, I need the means, not to do better than anyone else, but to promote my own identity in security and harmony. The great victory of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was to convince the Premiers to accept this sociological reality, and the miracle is that all of them agreed to consider the concept of a distinct society as an essential component of the Canadian federation. This is the great miracle of this Accord and this is also what makes it so delicate.
This is also why we rejected amendments which, while seeming to improve the Accord, could have destroyed it. It is not because we did not recognize that something must be done quickly in Canada for our native people. It is not because we refuse the right of francophones outside Quebec to develop fully. It is not because we are not sensitive to individual rights. It is not for those reasons, but because we know that it is impossible to do everything at once and that this basic component is essential for Quebecers. We heard the views of those who played a vigorous role in the Quebec referendum, of those who fought to keep Quebec within the Canadian Federation.
When I heard my Liberal friend speak about rights and the public interest earlier, it made me smile because it was under his Party that the country was nearly destroyed. It was because of his Party's philosophy of an ethereal centralizing federalism that Canada was nearly destroyed. It is true the country almost fell apart. It was very close.
I believe this Constitutional Accord is extremely important. I must say I am somewhat concerned about the kind of situation we have in New Brunswick, where a new Premier has just been elected with a crushing majority. It will be difficult in that province to have a parliamentary democracy that reflects public opinion, and I am particularly concerned about comments that, as far as Quebec is concerned, are quite hostile to this Constitutional Accord. I hope he will change his mind about making so-called improvements or changes. Otherwise, I am afraid they will all withdraw their signatures and their commitments. And that would be very serious indeed.
We all know it is extremely difficult to get everyone to agree on certain principles and ideas, to set aside personal perceptions and interests and sit down together and concentrate on the public interest and develop a united vision as nation
builders. It makes for a fragile Accord. But it also makes it important and fundamental and fascinating. It should not be tinkered with. If we tinker with this Accord, if we open it up again for the sake of making a few changes, it means releasing everyone from his commitment and his given word. And that is what we must understand.
Our committee understood this. We made about 20 recommendations with the future in mind, when further constitutional conferences will be held. We recommended setting up a standing constitutional committee that would make it possible to spend more time preparing agendas and subject matter. We are confident that in the future, despite the new unanimity rule-even if we did have the seven provinces and 50 percent rule, one cannot run a country by ramming issues down people's throats. One cannot do that. In any case, it takes a consensus and almost unanimous consent. In any case, it would take unanimous consent. It does in constitutional matters. It nearly always does, otherwise confrontation would be the order of the day.
Several witnesses said that if the Accord was not ratified as soon as possible by all parties involved, our Canadian federation might again be in jeopardy. People who do not believe that did not experience the events leading up to the Quebec referendum.
Granted, today Quebec has a government that has made a commitment to the Canadian federation. It is the same government that negotiated the basic elements of this Accord. It endorsed the Accord. And it sincerely hopes, and I am referring to the present Quebec Government, that the rest of Canada will do likewise.
In the future, it will still be possible to propose further amendments, this time with the approval of Quebec, which will participate gladly and show a great deal of interest, for instance, in the issue of Senate reform. And it will be more likely to consider proposals from eastern or western Canada.
I therefore feel that Hon. Members should read the Joint Committee report and in that sense I have a lot of admiration, Madam Speaker, for the position taken by the members of the New Democratic Party who, of course, express reservations and wishes, but who add: Our reservations will never result in destroying the agreement. What those people did, and what I would ask from my Liberal colleagues, both in the Senate and in the House of Commons eventually, would be to look at the Accord as being both fundamental and essential, although imperfect. This country's existence is at stake-not merely surviving but moving forward together as integral parts of this great country. And I would urge them to share that vision which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his colleagues have had of Canada, a vision of tolerance and respect for and promoting those creative differences.

Madam Speaker, in his comments the Hon. Member referred to the people of Quebec, Quebecers, as a small minority in a sea of some 250 million English-speaking
October 19, 1987

in North America, and I must confess I do not share his fears in that respect. I believe this small minority is much stronger perhaps than he is. We have the example indeed of the Lamarres, the Lorties, the Castonguays who are leading Quebec multinationals that are extending their activities around the globe. We also have the example of the 10 000 students each year who attend the Ecole des Hautes Etudes Commerciales in Montreal. And really, 1 am not under the impression that those people need the added protection of the distinct society concept.
Looking at the Eton. Member, Madam Speaker, I cannot help thinking either that he is quite a grown-up lad, and I would like to ask him why he needs that extra protection, that crutch as one might say, to stand on his own two feet?

Madam Speaker, 1 believe that it was the former Prime Minister who said-unfortunately, as is often the case, one of our own proved to be the most willing to bring us down-that Quebecers did not need any crutches such as this Accord. I do not consider the historic demands of Quebec to be crutches, and 1 do not consider that our will to create- and we did so by asserting ourselves and we did not wait for anyone else to do it for us. Otherwise, we would have disappeared a long time ago, my friend! 1 am quite happy to see that our small community, in close proximity to this majority of 250 million, was able, in the 25 years since the so-called quiet revolution, to obtain the tools necessary to develop and to produce competent men and women because of whom we can now open up to Canada, to the United States and to the rest of the world. There still remains that we had in Quebec a Government which was able to provide the necessary tools and to make enormous sacrifices-
You have full powers!
We gave ourselves as Quebecers-
You have no need for the Meech Lake Accord in that case!

One moment! 1 believe that you should reread your history books. You would see that, in spite of everything that has been said about our culture and our language and in spite of generous principles, it was because of this culture and this language that many of us were uprooted and became assimilated in this country. You say that we have no need for protection. The concept of a distinct society involves not only the protection, but also the promotion of this society, and this will enable us to do as much as we can.
