subtopic: TRIBUTE TO PERSONALITIES HONOURED, AND IN PARTICULAR TO MME LISE WATIER
TRIBUTE TO PERSONALITIES HONOURED, AND IN PARTICULAR TO MME LISE WATIER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week in Montreal the newspaper La Presse honoured six people at the Excellence 87 gala. The six personalities chosen were: Denys Arcand, film maker, Ben Johnson, sprinter, Dominique Michel, comedian, Claire L'Heureux-Dube, Supreme Court justice, Ludmilla Chiriaeff, founder of the Grands Ballets Canadiens and, finally, Mme Lise Watier, businesswoman. 1 would like to offer my warmest congratulations to each and every one of them.
Mr. Speaker, let me draw particular attention to the winner of that Excellence 87 award, Mme Watier. That dynamic businesswoman now owns, in the cosmetics field, an empire that spreads over more than 650 selling points in Canada and where she offers more than 450 products. And her business is constantly expanding. Indeed, Mme Watier has set her sights on first place in the cosmetics industry in Canada and would also like to penetrate foreign markets, those of the United States and Europe.
Mme Watier respects her male and female customers' tastes and needs. It is one of the reasons why the Watier Group is prospering so well. She is the symbol of the new wave of Quebec entrepreneurs who have won such renown at the national and international levels.
I know that all my colleagues in the House of Commons and particularly those from Quebec join with me to congratulate Mrs. Watier and wish her success in her future endeavours.

subsubtopic: STOCK MARKET COLLAPSE-EFFECT OF PROTECTIVE TARIFF WALLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the stock market collapse in New York, Toronto, London, Tokyo and Sydney reminds many of what happened in the 1930s. They should also be reminded of how that problem became a crisis because protective tariff walls were constructed not only around the United States but around Germany and many other countries.

October 19, 1987
It has become conventional wisdom for economists to say that the Depression of the 1930s might not have lasted so long or declined so deeply if free trade had been accepted in the 1930s. What about the 1980s and the 1990s? The same wisdom should show us that an expanding world population now gives us more than enough demand for our supply if we can only open up the channels of trade communication around the world.
Protection is the road to recession. Free trade offers the prospect of prosperity.

subtopic: AIDS DISEASE-THREATENED NON-TREATMENT OF VICTIMS BY DENTISTS
AIDS DISEASE-THREATENED NON-TREATMENT OF VICTIMS BY DENTISTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is tragic enough that the slow response of Governments to the AIDS crisis has allowed a climate of fear, ignorance and antipathy to homosexuals to produce such consequences as the recent abuse of human rights.
But it is a disgrace when members of the dental profession who should know better should, in such overwhelming numbers, state that they would refuse to treat AIDS victims. And when their professional organization advocates preventive measures against AIDS which are more consistent with the superstition of the dark ages than with modern microbiology and medicine, that is an outrage.
If dentists are so ill informed about elementary epidemiology, then it is clear that the practitioners of this lucrative health profession are ill trained and their patients ill served, and it is time for reform in their professional training.

subsubtopic: CRITICISM OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, have you noticed that the NDP rigidly adheres to any policy set out by the Canadian Labour Congress? For example, Shirley Carr stated that free trade was "selling Canada to the United States". Almost immediately the leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent) stated in the House "the Tories are selling Canada to the United States".
Again, the CLC supports the strike by the postal workers and so, are you surprised that the NDP holds up legislation forcing workers back to work for several days costing money for every small business in Canada, to say nothing about the inconvenience imposed on the people?
As a matter of fact, whenever there is a strike of union workers against the people, the NDP is on the side of the union. All of which begs the question: are MPs elected by the unions, or is it the healthy grant the unions pay to the NDP out of money contributed by all the union workers, many of whom never would and never will vote for a socialist candidate, the real reason? The people of Canada have a right to know.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF LOW WATER LEVELS ON BRITISH COLUMBIA SALMON SPAWNING GROUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a result of an extremely dry summer and fall in British Columbia fishermen, both sport and commercial, have expressed concern about the dry river beds, especially those containing prime salmon spawning grounds.
Low water levels in my riding have been recorded on the San Juan, Cowichan, Chemainus and Sooke Rivers, while on the mainland the Fraser River is at a near record low.
I recently toured the Cowichan River and saw first-hand the extremely low water level. The river has traditionally supported 3,500 to 7,000 Chinook salmon but these numbers have dwindled over the years. People fear that last year's record low of 1,200 returning spawners will be broken this year. To date only 400 have been counted by the local fisheries officer who was hoping to see 4,000. The situation is reaching crisis proportions as it is getting well into the spawning season.
While the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) cannot be expected to bring rain, he must provide increased funding for enforcement programs as well as river and stream enhancement programs to bring the stocks back to traditional levels, and he must guarantee the protection of fish habitat from the controllable forces of industrial polluters.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-SUPPORT FROM WHEAT AND LIVESTOCK PRODUCERS
CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-SUPPORT FROM WHEAT AND LIVESTOCK PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the real story on the effect free trade will have on the various sectors of our economy in Saskatchewan is being told, not by the left-leaning opposition Parties but by the producer groups themselves.
Bill Yeast, President of the Saskatchewan Stock Growers' Association, says we virtually have free trade with the U.S. in the beef industry already and this agreement will be very
October 19, 1987

important in maintaining our access to the U.S. market which in 1985 was worth over $250 million net to the beef industry.
Garth Larson, President of the Saskatchewan Pork Producers Marketing Board, recently stated that protectionism is our biggest problem and that this trade pact will ensure our accessibility to the U.S. market.
Bill Duke, President of the Western Canadian Wheat Growers Association, also stated that he thinks Canada now has a better chance of retaining current access and getting further access.
This is proof positive that the free trade agreement is a good deal and it will provide better certainty and security of access to the U.S. market for Canadian exporters. This is precisely what our Government set out to achieve.
 * *

Mr. Speaker, tourism is one of the most important industries in Canada. It generates hundreds of thousands of jobs and is worth $22 billion annually to our economy. Unfortunately, every year Canada experiences a tourism travel deficit. In fact, according to Tourism Canada, the travel deficit for this year is expected to increase significantly over last year.
For these and many other reasons, the Government should consider very seriously the implications of tax reform on the tourism industry. Canada must remain competitive. Increasing taxes on our tourism product will only make things worse.
In a recent appearance before the Commons committee on finance, the Tourism Industry Association of Canada had this to say:
If higher prices are encountered in the market-place due to the sales tax, the
hoped for increase in consumer spending will be compromised. If Canadians
perceive better value elsewhere, they will be quick to take advantage of it.
The Government should listen to this advice and utilize tax reform to increase the competitive position of Canada's important tourism industry.

subsubtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-CRITICISM OF NDP LEADER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we heard some more confusing rhetoric from the NDP over the weekend about the free trade issue, this time from none other
than their Leader, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent). We always thought that he and his Party were opposed to free trade. Yesterday he told the Council of Canadians that we should have included Mexico in the negotiations.
It seems members of the NDP believe in free trade as long as the negotiations do not include those horrible Americans.
There is even more evidence of double-speak. In the same speech, the Hon. Member for Oshawa suggested that Canada's preoccupation with the United States is costing Canada its share of very important traditional markets in western Europe-all this coming from a Party that wants to withdraw from NATO. What is that supposed to do, improve our access to European markets?
The fact is that what is good for Oshawa through the Auto Pact is good for the rest of Canada through free trade. It is good for British Columbia, it is good for Alberta, it is good for Saskatchewan, it is good for Manitoba and central Canada, it is good for the Maritimes, and it is good for Newfoundland.
No wonder the NDP has gone down 10 points in the polls in British Columbia and the Conservatives have gone up 10 points. They want an election on the free trade issue. Mr. Speaker, allons-y! Let's go!

subsubtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-CRITICISM OF NDP POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am fed up with the continual whining and snivelling of the NDP over free trade. From the Leader on down to Donald Wilson, the perennial NDP candidate in my riding, over and over they cry and complain that Canada will lose its sovereignty, that we cannot compete with the Americans, that the Americans will dictate our future, et cetera, et cetera, ad nauseam.
Is it because the American-controlled unions have long been the only support of the NDP? Have they no faith in Canada or Canadians? I have.
I firmly believe that Canadian manufacturers, producers, entrepreneurs, scientists, farmers and, yes, even Canadian union workers, can compete with any country in the world when barriers are removed and competition is equal. I have faith in Canada and this Party has faith in Canadians. Deliver us from weak-kneed, spineless socialists who have no faith in anything, perhaps not even in themselves.

October 19, 1987
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, after listening to the Conservatives attacking the NDP position on free trade 1 assume they have the confidence to call a national election. However, this afternoon I want to deal with a different issue.
I heard Peter Pocklington this morning speaking on CBC Radio telling the country that labour peace at the Post Office would be achieved through total privatization of the service. This seems to be typical of the Conservative mentality, but we are all familiar with Mr. Pocklington's concept of labour peace. In 1986 one of the most violent strikes in the private sector took place at Pocklington's Gainers plant in Edmonton. It was one of the most vicious anti-labour actions to occur in Canada in recent history. I remember the emotions felt amongst the strikers and their supporters across the country as busloads of scab workers crossed the union's legal picket line and did union work. We all know the stories about the scouring of men's hostels, welfare and unemployment ranks, looking for men and women to cross the picket line.
The Conservative Government created a postal business plan which includes franchising and ensures that thousands of union jobs, most done by women, will be replaced by people working at minimum wage. Obviously this appeals to the Pocklington mentality. With his history of labour relations Mr. Pocklington is being hypocritical in saying that privatization of the Post Office would ensure labour peace. He never had it in his own plant. He should also state that his vision of Canada is not one that recognizes many rights for the working people of Canada.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR GENERAL ELECTION ON PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE SUPPORTED FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statements we heard today from members of the Progressive Conservative Party would lead one to think they should have the courage of their convictions and do what they so often talk about with respect to parliamentary accountability and call an election on the free trade agreement.
It seems to me to be an apostasy of parliamentary accountability, particularly when it was so hard on a former Government for wanting to change the Constitution without a mandate, that that same Party now, when in government, should consider changing the economic constitution of Canada without a mandate from the people and without ever having mentioned such a thing in the election of 1984.
We are reminded of the Liberal hypocrisy in 1974 on another issue. This situation far surpasses that. We are talking about the future of Canada, and the Progressive Conservative
Party should have the guts to call an election on this free trade agreement.

subsubtopic: LAUNCHING OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AWARENESS WEEK
speechtext:
I am pleased to inform all Members that today marks the launch of House of Commons Awareness Week, a week of educational seminars and displays aimed at sensitizing Members and staff to the needs of the disabled, both as employees and visitors.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:

Has the Minister of Finance been in touch with the Secretary of the Treasury of the United States and his counterparts in Europe and Japan? Can he assure the House that there is an international support mechanism in place on a contingency basis?

I have looked with confidence at the performance of the Canadian economy during the early part of this year. During
October 19, 1987

the first half of the year the economy grew at 6 per cent in real terms which, I think the Hon. Member is quite well aware, is the leading performance among the major industrialized countries.

subtopic: STOCK MARKETS-EXCHANGE VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR
STOCK MARKETS-EXCHANGE VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Finance. It concerns the huge drop in the stock markets. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the Dow Jones industrial average dramatically plunged last week and the Toronto and Montreal Stock Exchange index also dropped proportionately. This morning the Toronto Stock Exchange dropped by 258 points, and just before coming into the House I found that the Dow Jones average had dropped by 300 points since the opening of the stock exchange this morning.
Since the dramatic fall of the stock market has convinced U.S. Secretary James Baker to say publicly that he will let the U.S. dollar fall against the Deutschmark and the currencies of other U.S. trading partners, what will the Canadian Government's policy be as far as the Canadian dollar is concerned in the face of this new U.S. policy? Will the Government favour a lower rate of interest to ensure that the Canadian dollar will not increase artificially, thereby damaging our competitiveness in the world market?

subtopic: STOCK MARKETS-EXCHANGE VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member is taking some liberties in interpreting what Secretary Baker said about the actions that have been taken in the German financial markets.
The specific question is related to the performance of the Canadian dollar and by implication, 1 believe, the level of interest rates and the activities in the bond market. As I indicated to the Hon. Member's colleague just a moment ago, there has been quite good stability in both the exchange markets and the bond markets this morning. I do not see any reason why we should try to take actions that anticipate something which might not happen. Let us watch to see how things develop before there is any precipitant action taken.

subtopic: STOCK MARKETS-EXCHANGE VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not trying to guess what is going to happen. The facts speak for themselves: a 500-point drop at the New York Stock Exchange, a proportional drop at both the Montreal and Toronto Stock Exchanges, something we have not seen since 1929. speechtext:

value of the American dollar drop against other currencies, and as a result the Canadian dollar edged up. subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT INTENDS TO PURSUE GRADUAL INCREASE IN INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me address the question the Hon. Member has put in relation to actions we have taken over the past two or three months in Canadian interest rates. Canadian interest rates have gone up. I think that is a reflection of the strong economy. As I indicated to his colleague, the economy in the first half of the year was the strongest of any of the major industrialized countries. There is a natural response of some increase and tightness of money because of the improvement in the economy.
The level of the dollar, though, I think has reflected some increased confidence in Canada as a result of that strong economic activity as well as the increased investment opportunities in Canada which have come about through programs this Government has introduced.
However, I think the level of the dollar and the level of interest rates are a good reflection of the relationships between Canada and the United States, our principal trading partner, as well as the level of economic activity which, as 1 said, has been very good in this country.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT WILL TAKE MEASURES TO REASSURE INVESTORS
INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT WILL TAKE MEASURES TO REASSURE INVESTORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Finance and has to do with the stock market drop, not only in New York and London but also at the Toronto and Montreal Stock Exchanges. subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT WILL TAKE MEASURES TO REASSURE INVESTORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is kind of interesting to see the New Democratic Party paying so much attention to the stock market.

speechtext: That is where they keep their money.

I do not want to make a lot of that because there is no question that the drops in the stock markets over the last little while have been quite large by historical standards. What I think we have seen over the past month or so is an indication of stock market analysts and economic analysts increasing their estimates of economic performance in Canada for the balance of the year and into next year. I think that it is much more important for us to look at the real aspects of the economy as opposed to the financial aspects of the economy as reflected in the stock market.
As I said in response to previous questions, I have a good deal of confidence in the current outlook for the Canadian economy. 1 do not believe that it is necessary to make precipitous changes in that since the economic and financial policies that we have been following have served us very well over the past three years.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER MEET BANKERS AND STOCK EXCHANGE OFFICIALS

Oh, oh!

States House of Representatives, led by the Hon. Tony Coehlo, the Hon. Dennis Hertel, the Hon. Sander Levin, and the Hon. Thomas Sawyer.

subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF DELEGATION FROM UNITED STATES HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of National Defence is tired of waving at the gallery, perhaps we will get on with the Question Period.
My question relates to a very serious issue. As we know, over the weekend U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Baker, who seems to take this matter more seriously than our Minister of Finance, indicated two things. First, they were going to review all previous agreements made by the Group of Seven, and look at how they could bring the U.S. currency down in relation to other currencies. The whole question of exchange rates has an enormous bearing upon the competitive value of Canadian resources and products that are sold to the United States.
I wish to ask the Minister of Finance in terms of the discussion that went on in the free trade agreement negotiations, what arrangements, agreements, or discussions took place in relation to the Canadian dollar? What type of understandings are there about whether we will continue to have total freedom to determine the value of our own dollar, and therefore keep our own exports competitive?

Mr. Speaker, there is nothing at all in the free trade agreement that has anything to do with the levels of the Canadian dollar, the U.S. dollar, and the relationship. On a continuing basis we have made the point, as has the Secretary of the Treasury, that it is markets that control exchange rates.
We as part of the Group of Seven-which I should point out the Hon. Member's Government was not a part of, so he would not understand the nature of discussions that we had-at the end of September had a full discussion at the G-7 meeting which looked at a number of the outlooks for the different countries. In that forum we received a good understanding of the expectations for the international economy. I should say that the expectations were quite positive.

Mr. Speaker, the expectations may have been positive, but the results on the stock market today are not so positive.
I wish to ask the Minister of Finance about a statement made over one year ago by the then Minister for International Trade of the Conservative Government. When asked a

October 19, 1987
Oral Questions
question by my colleague about the relationship between the value of the dollar-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Which colleague?
The Hon. Member for Saint-Henri- Westmount.
Oh, oh!

-and about the question of exchange rates, the then Minister for International Trade stated, "It is certainly something we are very conscious of and we are prepared to enter these negotiations and we will have to have those discussions with the United States".
I wish to ask the Minister of Finance, if that was the intention of the then Minister for International Trade, would he tell us what discussions were held with the United States on the question of the value of the dollar? Will we find ourselves caught in the same position as the Israelis when they signed an agreement that they had to peg their dollar to the United States dollar? What types of arrangements and discussions have been held between the two countries in relation to the free trade arrangement and the value of our respective currencies?

Mr. Speaker, the substance of those discussions is carried out in the international forum of the G-7. There are seven countries there, each of which discusses the outlook for its economy, and from time to time the relationship of its currency to the other countries is a subject of those discussions.
I have said in the House on many occasions that the level of the Canadian dollar is a level that is set by the market-place. There have been a number of Senators who have made comments on this, and I tell those people in the United States when I meet them face to face, or through Secretary Baker, that it is not our policy to establish a fixed level for the Canadian dollar. It is not our policy to manage in a so-called "dirty float" a level for the Canadian dollar. We lean into the market going both ways, but that is only to moderate the movements in the market-place. That is the policy of this Government, and it is fully understood by representatives of the United States Government.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-BILL C-22- WASHINGTON NEWSPAPER REPORT

a section pledging Canada to change its drug patent laws, administration and industry sources said yesterday".

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am surprised that the Hon. Member did not read the full article which stated, "The United States bowed to Canadian demands-"

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-BILL C-22- WASHINGTON NEWSPAPER REPORT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-BILL C-22- WASHINGTON NEWSPAPER REPORT

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-BILL C-22- WASHINGTON NEWSPAPER REPORT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised that the Minister did not read the whole article which goes on to state, "Reagan administration sources who were close to the final negotiations said the drug issue was part of the deal when Wilson stepped to the window of the Treasury building just before midnight Saturday and gave a thumbs-up sign to signal there was an agreement".

Mr. Speaker, I am not quite sure I got the last part of the Hon. Member's question.
Surely the Hon. Member knows that on many occasions we have stated our intention to pass Bill C-22.
October 19, 1987

We have stated it on many occasions to the United States, to the Germans, to the Swiss, to the French, and that is a statement of our government policy. Our policy related to pharmaceutical patent protection was part of our policy in the last election. It has been a part of the direction of the Government for a number of months now. We have stated consistently, publicly, privately, formally, informally, verbally, and in writing that it remains our intention to pass Bill C-22.
That is a statement of fact. It is a simple statement of the obvious. We passed it twice already in this House.

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the House adjourned at 1:00 p.m., there were six minutes left from the question and comment period, following the speech made by the Hon. Member for Charlevoix (Mr. Hamelin).

I will now recognize Hon. Members who wish to continue the question and comment period. Since there are no questions or comments, continuing debate.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to have the opportunity to speak on this resolution. Being a Member of Parliament is sometimes very frustrating and very difficult. Then, of course, there are times when one is working on something with which one has a tremendous affinity, something in which one believes very strongly.
When I was elected in 1979 it was the position of this Party that we would work toward one Canada, a Canada with two founding peoples, two cultures, two main languages, but one
Constitution Amendment, 1987
country. We had dismissed the notion of deux nations and we were moving toward something which we felt would be a mainstay for the future. Not only was it helpful to Canada in maintaining unity and developing a singleness of purpose so that Canadians of French and English origin could be at home anywhere in this country, but it was something that would move away from the prejudices and divisions about which we had worried for so long.
In this the 20th century I think our main concern is that we now have a technology that to a large extent is still governed by 19th century prejudices and shortsightedness. The sophistication of weapons, the nationalism and the religion were superimposed upon the prejudices and fears that we want so much to dispel in this century. Now this dream of one Canada is being thrown away. We will not be able to have that goal to shoot for.

I believe the principle of two founding people and two languages is extremely important to this country, Canada.
Quebec where most of our francophone fellow citizens live surely deserves special attention, but each and every one of our provinces is different from the others. Of course, and I say it publicly, all my Liberal colleagues from Quebec are my friends and I can very well understand their position in this regard. But everyone knows there are francophones and Anglophones all over this country.
We all know for instance that Quebec City was founded in 1608 four years after the founding of Port-Royal. The federal Government must help Acadians preserve their culture. With this agreement, Acadian culture may vanish in a few years, particularly in the provinces of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island.

All members of this Party are interested in seeing Quebec as a signatory to the Constitution of this country. I do not think there is anything in politics that I want to see more, because it is necessary to complete the constitutional picture of this country. However, there are times when this just cannot be achieved.
At the meeting on April 30 a difficulty was presented. I think Quebec could have come into the Constitution. 1 think it is very important that it does so, but the problem is with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). The problem is that the Prime Minister was not representing the federal Government. There was no federal presence at that table.
While we could have achieved at that meeting the objectives that Quebec wanted and still have maintained a unified thrust with respect to the Meech Lake Accord, when the other provinces saw an undefended federal caucus they themselves became anxious to obtain other objectives. The federal Government gave more than it was asked for by the Province of Quebec. It is not necessarily wrong to give the provinces additional powers. The question is, what are those additional

October 19, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
powers going to be. What is going to be left for the federal Government?
For example, federal spending power is very important. There are programs which have to be implemented universally. We saw that with the Canada Pension Plan and the Canada Health Act. There might be similar programs in the future regarding education, training, or perhaps for doing away with illiteracy before too long. Can that be achieved if the provinces have the right to bail out of those programs? That can happen because provinces can opt out and receive compensations so long as their programs achieve national objectives.
What are these national objectives going to be? We do not know. We do not even know how we are going to define "national objectives". Under the Meech Lake Accord it may be that the federal Government will not have the right to define national objectives. They will have to be defined at First Ministers' Conferences. What kind of position are we going to be in then? What kind of position are we going to be in if it is not Government by this Parliament but Government by First Ministers?
It is important to have consultation with the provinces-very important. It should be maintained, yet not to the extent we have developed it in this country. I imagine that the provinces, during the meetings at Meech Lake, could not believe their ears when they were offered what they were offered. They were probably like 10 children who see an overturned ice cream truck.
In the body of the Meech Lake Accord there is a stipulation that there will be meetings to determine jurisdiction over the fishery. It does not say that this issue will be brought up at the next First Ministers' Conference. It says it will be brought up. It seems to me that the implication is it will be brought up continually until it is resolved. That could mean that Newfoundland will achieve its hopes for jurisdiction over fishing areas adjacent to it. That would be devastating to other provinces in Atlantic Canada. Even now the fishing industry in Nova Scotia is hesitant about investing because they do not know what this clause will mean. Why should it be in the constitutional document? It is an agenda item and it should not be there.
Western Canada is hopeful that the Senate will be reorganized and we will have a Triple-E Senate. How will that happen when all provinces have to agree to changes in the Senate? They also have to agree on the creation of new provinces. How will the Yukon and the Northwest Territories become provinces when the existing provinces and the federal Government must unanimously agree?
Then we have the Supreme Court. As with the Senators, the Supreme Court has to be chosen from a list submitted by the respective provinces and agreed to by the federal Government. If you have a Government of one political Party in the province and another political Party federally, it is going to be
very difficult to make a selection. What happens when a province is not interested in achieving unanimity? I do not say that is going to happen, but we must look at the possibility. The Supreme Court is the glue of our Constitution and as such is tremendously important.
The federal system is extremely important. We have in Canada now one of the most decentralized federal systems in the world. We cannot allow it to become more so or this country will become ungovernable. The tendency will be towards a splitting and splintering of our federal system. It is no good for the Prime Minister to say we are going to have consultation and a meeting of minds. That is like General Custer at the Little Bighorn saying he now has the Sioux nation where he wants them. It is just not possible. Either you have a Constitution which defines the country you want or you do not.
A Constitution is inviolate. You cannot change it at will, the way you can change legislation. That is something we have to think very long and very hard about. It cannot be the result simply of the fact that the Prime Minister was able to stay up later than most of the others involved. It has to be something with which we can work.
If Members of this place can truly say that this is the Canada they want, I can live with that. What I cannot accept is Members of this House saying they do not like this, that they have to hold their noses, but they are going to vote for it anyway. I said before, and I will say it again and again and again, that there is nothing I want more than to have Quebec as a signatory to our Constitution and a member of this confederation. That is something I have always worked towards. However, we have to be careful that we do not deviate so far from the path that we cannot get back on. We must have control over it.
It is not a very pleasant thing for me to say that I cannot support this Accord. I will be considered as a Liberal Member who does not support his Leader. Nothing could be further from the truth. 1 support him completely. I have tremendous respect for him. It is just that I have difficulty seeing this Accord as maintaining the Canada and the constitutional framework for which I have worked for eight years. It is also important that each person state his or her beliefs. Canada requires, more than anything else, honesty from politicians, the people who have some say over whether or not this Accord is passed. If we had that, that is fine. But, if in that meeting of First Ministers at Meech Lake certain Premiers went along for the sake of going along, that is not consensus as I know it. Consensus means acting in the best interests of all parties and building a stronger Canada, not a political Canada in which provinces believe that it is good for them to have more power.
Former Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau said that he understood the position of the provinces. He did not agree with the Meech Lake Accord but understood the position of the
October 19, 1987

provinces because politics is achieving power. He was very kind and I think that position is understandable. However, it can only be condoned if the Premiers really believed that this will be good not only for the provinces but for Canada as a whole. In my opinion that has not been the result.
As this debate winds down it is very important that everyone who has a chance to speak on this very important resolution to ask who is speaking for Canada. Madam Speaker, Members of Parliament who vote against this resolution speak for Canada.

Madam Speaker, for all of the reasons mentioned by my good friend, the Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan), I am highly in favour of the Meech Lake Accord. I come from a far outpost of the empire, as he does, from Vancouver, which is a very long way from Ottawa. Too long in western Canada we have seen central Canada decide that central Canada is one Canada and that what is good for Ontario and Quebec is good for the rest of us. We have seen many incidents and I do not want to refer to all of them. However, central Canada's demands in the early 1980s that the oil industry in the West subsidize Ontario was devastating to our economy.
I like First Ministers' Conferences. First Ministers' Conferences have really been the only opportunity for the western provinces and the smaller provinces to have an equal say in what happens in Canada. Eleven people sit around a table. We have a representative there from British Columbia. Alberta has one representative, as has Ontario, Quebec and the other provinces. They are all equal at that table.
The Member suggested that the Constitution should not be changed easily. I agree with that. Unless any change in the Constitution is in the best interests of the entire country, it will not be changed. I agree with that as well.
Too long we have suffered from what I call the 75-95 syndrome, 75 seats in Quebec and 95 seats in Ontario. If you have those two provinces in agreement you can ignore the rest of the country. The 28 Members from British Columbia do not have too much impact. I say that in a non-partisan sense. My friends from British Columbia in the New Democratic Party, the Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), and the 19 Conservative Members from British Columbia are all interested in what is best for our province as well as what is best for the country. Obviously there are differences of opinion about what is best for the country.
The argument over the Meech Lake Accord is really a philosophical argument. It depends on whether you believe in a unitary state with all decisions being made in the centre, or whether you believe that government should be as close to the people it concerns as possible. I believe that the best government is the government that is closest to the people. I see no similarity between the outposts of Newfoundland and the lower mainland of British Columbia. I see very little agreement between the prairie wheat farmer and the industrialist in southern Ontario. This is one huge country; very broad, very
Constitution Amendment, 1987
long, very big. Let us get government to the regions so that people can decide for themselves.
The Member spoke of national programs. Remember that under the Meech Lake Accord a province may opt out of a national program but must provide the equivalent of that program and serve its people in the best way it can. That is fair enough.
Quebec is entitled to its own legitimate concerns. Quebec is a unique society. I am delighted that Quebec signed the Meech Lake Accord and delighted that it will be able to run its own affairs in the way it wishes, particularly with regard to culture. Those are the decisions of Quebec and should not be made by someone from British Columbia or Ontario. The same applies right across this vast country.
With regard to a loss of power to Parliament, I believe that Parliament should lose a lot of its power. Anyone who argues against that does not understand the geography of Canada. In a country 4,000 miles wide it is obvious that the regions are considerably different, one from another. The regions should have much more say about what will happen in them. Programs that are suitable for Atlantic Canada are often totally unsuitable for British Columbia. I like the federal conference of the First Ministers which gives one province one vote.
It is suggested that the Senate will never be reformed. I suggest that there is such a demand in this country for Senate reform that the First Ministers will come to an agreement but, again, each province will have an equal say as to what that agreement will be.
It is a very dangerous thing for a Premier to go against his colleagues for narrow interests and then have to return home, because he is responsible to the public and has to seek reelection, whereas the Senator does not. We will have Senate reform and it will come about through the First Ministers.
Frankly, the Meech Lake Accord is the best thing that has happened to this country in a very long time. Those opposed to it are looking at narrow power bases and that is not what will hold this country together. This country will be held together by more diffusion of power to the regions, where it should be on very many issues.

Madam Speaker, there is a lot in what the Hon. Member has stated. As he mentioned, we have been friends for a long time. This, of course, is only a disagreement.
I do not think this is a philosophical argument. This argument goes to the core of how one believes that the country's Constitution and framework should be structured.
The Hon. Member said that he favours government by First Ministers which gives the regions a greater say. Coming from Atlantic Canada, as I do, I can appreciate that. However, I balk at the suggestion that we can give the regions more say only through the First Ministers. I am afraid that if the First Ministers are allowed to control they will have a conflict of interest They are, first and foremost, the leaders of their own

October 19, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
provinces. That is what they were elected to be. We would be superimposing upon them a second duty, that is, to act in the national interests. That is not necessarily compatible with the best interests of their own provinces.
If a Premier wants to act in accordance with his role as the Premier of his province, as is understandable, his attitude toward the federal and unified central Government becomes political. We then get into linkages, trade-offs, and bargaining with regard to what the various Premiers want. You get a shopping list and that shopping list is then split up. That is what I am afraid of. If we do not have a strong central government, we do not have the opportunity to have a body which has one obligation, one elected responsibility, and that is to speak on behalf of this whole country. If the Hon. Member has stated honestly-and I believe he has-his intention, then I believe he will be voting the right way, to support the Meech Lake Accord. I respect his opinion and I am not going to try to change his mind. We just disagree.

speechtext: I regret, but the time for questions and comments has now finished. Resuming debate.

Madam Speaker, before I start, I may as well make the statement I wanted to make after listening very carefully to the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan). He ended up by saying that those who would be voting no in this House are for Canada. I think on reflection he may admit he got carried away with his rhetoric. In fact, he is saying to the rest of us who are going to vote, with just as much passion, for the Meech Lake Accord, that somehow or other we are not for Canada. I think if he reflects on that he will see that he is not speaking necessarily for all Canadians in this House, true and blue, true and pink or true and red.
I am delighted I have this opportunity to participate in a constitutional debate about Canada. God knows, I wanted to do so in 1982, but as fate and the people of Nickel Belt would have it, I was not here to participate.
As I watched the debate from the sidelines, there were things I wanted to say. There were things on my mind I wanted to say about my country and about my vision of Canada and where we should be headed. That is basically what I want to start off with. I have a vision of this country, a country that occupies the northern half of North America, a country that is indeed strong and free to develop its culture, economy and all the attributes of its people in the way we see fit. I have a vision of a Canada that goes back and corrects the injustices that were done to the original inhabitants of this land. Surely, if one were to read history, one would admit in all
conscience that in fact we have not dealt justly with the original inhabitants of this part of North America.
I have a vision of a country that is free to select those who shall govern. I have a vision of Canada where its people live in harmony with its vast resources, where its people understand the finite nature of these resources and in fact emulate the original inhabitants and try to live in harmony with this vast wilderness and the vast resources which are ours. I have a vision of this country that the quality of life of all its people is far more important than the quantity of life of a few. Perhaps that is where my socialism comes in.
I see a nation that is capable and able to provide a quality of life that is an example to the world and not a carbon copy of the atavistic, selfish nature I see so often depicted in the land south of our country. I have a vision of this country that encourages the living diversity which is the multicultural complexity of Canada. In fact, we not only want to encourage it, we want to ensure it grows, matures and contributes to the developing of the finest country in the world. That is my vision.
I see the Meech Lake Accord in two aspects within that vision, like a thread through the mosaic. The first aspect is Quebec. We all recall 1980. I had an opportunity to watch from the sidelines and I recall, when the moment of decision was approaching for the people of Quebec to vote "oui ou non", that Canadians were reaffirming their desire for Quebec to stay in Canada. We were saying all sorts of things which we have forgotten. There was a group called People-to-People which circulated a petition from coast to coast with 800,000 names which said "we love you Quebec. Stay in the family. Do not seek sovereignty association". The petition was given to Mayor Drapeau of Quebec. We were in love. It was a love that had been dimmed by time. We suddenly discovered that we loved Quebec and wanted Quebec to stay within the family. Canadian political leaders of all stripes were reaching out to Quebec. I can name some of them. There was Claude Ryan, Jean Chretien, Pierre Trudeau, the Opposition Leader at that time, now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), the Leader of one of the opposition Parties, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), Allan Blakeney and a whole host of provincial Premiers. They all said: "Stay in the family". Legislatures in our provinces, which often in the past were seen as hostile, discovered the new love relationship, and Alberta and British Columbia unanimously passed resolutions calling for Quebec to stay in Canada and for "a new federalism".
Most important, the federal Liberal Government promised constitutional changes in the wake of the referendum because Quebec voted no. It voted for Canada. Pierre Trudeau, the day after the referendum in May, 1980-I turned on my radio and there he was, thumbs in his belt-said:
All together what Quebecers expressed yesterday was a massive support for change within the federal framework. We cannot venture to ignore this will to change which reflects that of all other areas of the country and to fall short of the expectations of Canadians.
October 19, 1987

Madam Speaker, as Pierre Trudeau said later in this same speech: "Those voters said no because they put their confidence in Canada".
We all know that two years later the dust of time has started to cover over the love relationship again. As so often happens, love turns stale, and two years later they forget. They forget this marvellous Gallic lover across the Ottawa River, forget her completely. The rose is off the bloom. Out of sight, out of mind. Canada got what she wanted, kicked Quebec out of the bed. That is the way it goes in every love affair.
Two years later the Trudeau Government and nine provini-cial leaders signed the Constitution. So, in fact, we have had a Constitution for these last five years that shut out our lover, shut out one of the most important ingredients in the constitutional family-Quebec. She was left out in the cold. I think that the Meech Lake Accord attempts to correct that. I think the Meech Lake Accord has done that. The Meech Lake Accord has gone back and said to Quebec, "You belong in the constitutional family. Come and take your rightful place at the table with the rest of the brothers and sisters in the constitutional family".
For me, that is a thread through this vision of Canada that is important. It is important because one understands that to negotiate means that sometimes one has to give up to get. That is what Pierre Trudeau never understood.
This is the second reason that I support Meech Lake, and there is no quibbling about it-it is not "I am for it but-" or "I am against it but I will vote for it", none of that. I will tell Hon. Members the second reason. It is that this is a new era. Gone are the days of the gun-slinger with his thumbs stuck in his belt saying, "It is my way or the highway", someone who had no respect for provincial Premiers, or no respect for MPs who were nobodies 300 feet off the Hill.
His interview with The Toronto Star was a prime example of reason over emotion. In that article in The Toronto Star he called the Premiers all sorts of names. He called the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) a name. This is a person who was unable to get agreement with Quebec in 1982. I am not surprised. For me, the Meech Lake Accord is not only a yes vote to Quebec but it is the dawning of a new era in Canadian federalism.
We have an agreement which is more in line with reality in Canada today. As I have travelled it seems to me that people in northern Ontario, in Atlantic Canada, in western Canada, have always felt disconnected from the whole. They always felt there was some great conspiracy in central Canada, that southern Ontario and Quebec could cook things up and freeze them out. I know that, that is what we feel in northern Ontario. We all feel it about Queen's Park in Toronto. I know the whole country feels it about Toronto. That is the reality. In many ways this Accord reaffirms the original vision of John A. Macdonald. As we read history we know that he was a great
Constitution Amendment, 1987
centralist. He believed that the central Government should have all the power. But he had to back away from that concept because of the pressure from the leaders in the provinces at the time and from people in general. So he had to back away.
We know that the socio-economic reality of this country and, indeed, the geographic reality of this country, demands more decentralized decision-making. It needs to be more flexible and responsive to the aspirations of those of us who live in the hinterlands, who live far away from the Windsor-Quebec corridor.
I think Eric Kierans put it correctly when he said:
To recognize that the provinces are independent and autonomous in their own areas of jurisdiction takes Canada off the fast track of centralism that would have as its final stop "sovereignty association".
That is the direction in which the Meech Lake Accord is going-decentralization of the power of the central Government. I have no problem with that.
It seems to me that it recognizes that flexibility which says that what is good for Newfoundland may not be good for Alberta, or B.C., or Ontario. It also allows that what is good for Ontario and Quebec is not necessarily good for the Atlantic region, or for the West.
It seems to me that the Meech Lake Accord fulfils and is that thread through this vision that I have of Canada and that in fact it is more democratic. It is open, more responsive and attentive to regional minorities. This is my reading of it. This is how I see it.
It seems to me that the case for Meech Lake was made by Pierre Elliott Trudeau in 1961. In fact, he is now the guru of those who are going to vote no. Here is what Pierre Trudeau said in 1961:
In the age of the mass society, it is no small advantage to foster the creation of quasi-sovereign communities at the provincial level, where power is much less remote from the people and where political education and general creativeness is related to a more homogeneous and manageable group of citizens.
He makes the argument and, in fact, it is an important argument, one I have always felt was essential for a country this size geographically speaking. In fact, we have to keep that power as close to the people as possible, to the people who have to live with the laws.
Contrast that vision that Trudeau had in 1961 with his actual performance when in office as Prime Minister of this country. I remember well his arrogance and his elitism in this House and outside the House. I remember the way he handled workers, the working class people of this nation, the Lapalme postal workers. We remember his famous words. We remember this giant who believes now in a strong central Government. We heard him. We remember his words, "Why should I sell your wheat?" Those were the words of a person who believed in reason over emotion. I said before, Madam Speaker,

October 19, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
that here is a person who believed in reason over emotion. He described the drafters of Meech Lake as "eunuchs" and "weaklings". He decried provincial leaders and Quebec nationalists as "perpetual losers who don't have the stature of vision to dominate the Canadian stage". All this from someone who gave us a perfect example of how collegiality works, of how to negotiate, of what co-operative federalism was all about.
We know that that type of bulwark federalism leads to the type of descriptions we have had of provincial leaders who consistently play off against the federal leadership. We saw that in Alberta and in Newfoundland. In fact, it is this type of bulwark central Government that has led to that type of small provincial politics that is often played in this country.
We all remember an earlier Trudeau who displayed more common sense when he was a CCFer than when he was a Liberal. He stated:
It is perhaps no coincidence that during the twentieth century, the one party that was the strongest and governed longest is the party that has traditionally stood for provincial rights and embraced in its ranks such provincial free stylers as Taschereau, Hepburn, Angus MacDonald, and Smallwood.
In closing, I wish to state that mine is a full commitment to Meech Lake. I will vote for it. I recognize that we are in our infancy of constitution-making. I see the Meech Lake document as being very fluid as opposed to static. First, it is important to have the family at the table. In the years to come, we can work on making it a more reflective and sensitive document for all the reasons that many Members have stated, and for whatever has been left out. I believe that I speak as an optimist when I say that. I am not pessimistic about Canada. I am optimistic. Whether I like it or not, the Premiers of the provinces are elected by the same people who elect you and me, so it is an exercise of democracy. With goodwill and cooperative federalism we must sit around the table and continue to make our Constitution a living and a maturing document that serves Canadians and not one that Canadians serve.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is always a pleasure to be in the House when our friend the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) delivers a speech, because he is full of life, voluble, and very interesting to listen to.
Madam Speaker, I was all the more interested that, throughout his speech, the Hon. Member paid tribute to our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). The Hon. Member said: If you compare Mr. Trudeau's vision of Canada and that of our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) . . . From what I heard of the Hon. Member's speech, I concluded that our Prime Minister was fantastic; he is a man whose vision of Canada is in line with our times, and different from Mr. Trudeau's vision at the time when he wanted to control everything and leave no powers to the provinces.
In addition, the Hon. Member admits that we are going through periods when-it is a fact in my own riding and I
guess it is the same in yours, Madam Speaker-our constituents want to take more part in the decision-making process. Let us only think, for instance, of the Regional Industrial Development Program. I am sure that the voters of Nickel Belt will say: We know what we want in our region; and in Ottawa you are too far away from our ridings, therefore you cannot know precisely what is happening.
I would therefore like to congratulate the Hon. Member who is going to vote for the Meech Lake Accord and I would ask him to tell me as well whether he does recognize the unprecedented leadership shown by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who has been able to conclude a historical agreement at Meech Lake, to bring ten premiers to vote for and agree to the inclusion of Quebec in the Constitution. Does the Hon. Member admit that for the first time in Canada's history, a prime minister has successfully attempted that? Second, how does the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt explain in his own words, for instance, how a member of this House, particularly one from Quebec, the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger), said that he intended to vote against the Meech Lake Accord . . . Could the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt make some comments about the fact that a member from Quebec is voting against the Meech Lake Accord?

Madam Speaker, first, I wish to thank the Hon. Member for her kind comments. The Hon. Member asked if I would admit that the Prime Minister has done a fantastic job, and so forth. That is another part of the vision that I have of Canada. One person does not go around taking glory for things that have been done in the name of Canada. It takes 10 provinces plus a Prime Minister to make a deal. First, I did not rise to blow the horn for the Prime Minister. I was not head of the parade for his fan club.
One of the things I have learned around here is to give credit. The Prime Minister showed some leadership on this particular issue, the Meech Lake Accord, yes. I give credit where credit is due, because I am also critical when I think there is a reason for criticism. I give the Prime Minister credit for the leadership he exhibited, but I also give credit to the other Premiers who sat around the table to make a deal.
I have real concern about the fact that the same type of leadership was not shown when it came to discussing free trade. We can sign all the Meech Lake agreements that we wish. I have this vision of Canada. But not to turn around, as the Prime Minister is about to do with the free trade agreement, because he knows how to run a branch plant as he did for the Iron Ore Company of Canada in Schefferville where we all know what happened. It was closed down, everyone received the appropriate settlement, and the last one to leave put out the lights.
I wish to caution the Hon. Member that while I say it was a job well done, we stand the risk on the free trade deal of losing the whole ball of wax. We put in jeopardy the vision of Canada that I have, and I will be extremely critical when we come into
October 19, 1987

debate on that matter. But I wish to say here and now that, yes, the Prime Minister did a good job on this, he showed leadership as did the other Premiers. I think it is a document worth supporting.

The Hon. Member is to be congratulated for his remarks. They were made with his usual passion and brio. Unfortunately, there are only a few Members who are present for this debate on Meech Lake. I do not think that the Hon. Member was present when I spoke-
I listened to it on television.

The Hon. Member states that he listened to it on television. Very good.

I would also invite the member from Quebec to read my statements. She might find the answer to the question she asked.

The Hon. Member has a vision and view of history. He will accept that others have a different vision and perhaps a different view of history. The Hon. Member went through the 1980 referendum and stated that he watched it and participated in it par personae interposee. I was there and 1 participated in it in my constituency in the east end of Montreal. He quoted Mr. Trudeau who, on the day after the referendum, said that Quebecers voted no because they put their confidence in Canada. I would suggest to him that the operative words of that statement are "in Canada". That is precisely what makes us feel uneasy about the Meech Lake agreement. In my opinion it reverses the policies of the past 25 years, which were designed to make Quebecers and French Canadians feel at home in Canada, in all parts of Canada. French Canadians should not feel that they are somehow limited to la societe distincte de la province de Quebec.
I invite the Hon. Member to understand my reasoning for feeling that Meech Lake is a step backward. If we look at what was done over the years, with the Official Languages Act and Sections 16 to 23 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, it substantially enhanced linguistic rights above and beyond what was contained at the time of Confederation in Sections 93 and 133 of the BN A Act, 1867. Indeed there was constitutional change as a result of the referendum, and that was represented in the 1981 Constitution and the Charter of Rights. However, Meech Lake reverses that trend, and the rights which were inscribed in our 1981 Constitution will now be weakened as a result of the Meech Lake agreement.

Madam Speaker, I welcome the comments of the Hon. Member. I can give him the assurance-but I
Adjournment Debate
know that he will not take it-that I have read the Meech Lake Accord and I do not see one iota, one sentence, or one dot or tittle, as the Minister would say, in the agreement which would limit Quebecers from moving anywhere in the country. In fact, the Hon. Member may not be aware of the realities in places like my riding where, for example, 40 per cent of my constituents are Francophone. Over the last 10 years or 15 years I have seen the development within northeastern Ontario of an infrastructure of elementary and secondary French schools. I have seen the development of courts in the French language. I have seen an awakening in the French language in other parts of the country. It seems to me that Meech Lake in fact reinforces that.
Quebec is now sitting around the table. As we want to enhance the Constitution, it is important to have Quebec there. If my hon. friend had his way, I suspect that the alternative to Meech Lake would be to say to Quebec, "Stay out in the wilderness, stay out in the darkness", where it will be weeping and gnashing its teeth for another five years while they continue to impose the notwithstanding clause. As long as we have the family together, the family which discusses and changes together is the family that will stay together. That is my advice to the Hon. Member.
I appeal to him to reconsider his position. In fact, it is very important for Quebec to know that we meant what we said in 1980, when we said to Quebec: "Join the family and we will make right by you".
Quebec is a distinct society, communally, historically, and linguistically. I have no problem with that. I appeal to the Hon. Member who comes from the Province of Quebec to show some leadership and come with the rest of us as we say that this is a second step in a long road of constitution-making together as a family.
