speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is an important day for me where I have an opportunity to take part in the debate on the Meech Lake Accord, and the day that historic Accord was signed was a memorable one for the electors of the riding of Trois-Rivieres, as for everyone in Quebec and the country.
Madam Speaker, let me first congratulate the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) whose excellent work in this historic issue was mentioned several times by Members and Ministers of the Government as well as Members, 1 think, of both opposition Parties. I wish to congratulate also the 10 Premiers who agreed to sit at the same table and who made that agreement, the Joint Senate and Commons Committee who did a tremendous job, in my opinion.
You know, Madam Speaker, when we were elected in 1984, the idea that came to mind when the name Meech Lake was mentioned was that of a place of rest and relaxation. But since the Accord, the words Meech Lake are synonymous with historic agreement. It means team work. It means a great country, Canada, is finally united. I think it is extremely important to have a united country while at the same time respecting Quebec's character as a distinct society. You know as well as I do that Quebec is truly a distinct society within Canada. It is a fact, it has been, is and will be part of our experience. And the 10 premiers representing four different political formations, along with the Prime Minister of Canada, acknowledged that fact, without any partisanship. With the result that Quebec which was entitled to a seat at the constitutional meetings will now have it, a good thing for that province, for Canada and also for all socio-economic and cultural decision-makers who will be able to make progress and think from now on about Canada not as it was in 1982 or 1981 or 1971, but as it is in 1987, that is a country with 10 provinces.
To say that the Meech Lake Accord is not perfect, that changes or such and such amendment should be made, quite simply, Madam Speaker, is to express rejection of the Accord. There has been an agreement. As the Canadian Government, we must sign it as must the 10 provinces. There will be a second round. There will be a second stage where, once again, the 10 Premiers and the Prime Minister of Canada will meet, reassess the situation, improve the Accord if need be, as I think is perfectly normal and logical, but a first step has been taken. We must respect it and sign that Accord as soon as possible to
be able to go forward, to consider more changes in the future, because not to sign it would bring us back to 1982. In 1982, the Constitution was patriated, not only without the consent of the Quebec Government of the day, but without the consent of the whole National Assembly. It was not a partisan issue, not something about Quebec separating, because the Party in power was a separatist one. The whole National Assembly had refused. And as you know, Madam Speaker, a good number of those in the Opposition were Members of the Quebec Liberal Party. This is something we should keep in mind when we talk about this in 1987 and when we realize the progress that has been made and the point that has been reached.
Madam Speaker, we are making good the mistakes of 1982, as the Prime Minister had promised he would in a speech he made in Sept-Iles during the 1984 election campaign. If I may, for the purpose of this debate, I should like to read part of the speech the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made in Sept-Iles. He said: One thing is sure: No Quebecer has authorized the Liberal Party in Ottawa to take advantage of Quebec's utter confusion following the referendum to ostracize it constitutionally. My Party finds no pleasure in the political morass in which these deplorable events have placed Quebec. If Quebec is weak, Canada is weak too. If Quebec is strong, so is Canada. There is a place in Canada for the affirmation of all identities, for the respect of all aspirations and for the pursuit of all ideals. I know that many Quebecers will not be satisfied with mere words. It will be necessary to take action to reach the objectives which 1 have assigned for myself and which I repeat here: To convince Quebec's National Assembly to give its consent with honour and enthusiasm to the new Canadian Constitution.
Madam Speaker, those were the Prime Minister's words in 1984, in Sept-Iles, during the election campaign. The Meech Lake Accord is the very reflection of the Prime Minister's promise made in 1984, and it does not reflect it simply because he made it as a Prime Minister, but because of the fact that the 10 Premiers climbed on the bandwagon. And that, in my view, is important.
You certainly remember, Madam Speaker, before you were elected, the situation surely was the same in your constituency as in mine and in a number of others across Canada, especially in Quebec-our MLA's would only speak to our MP's through the media. The only way they spoke to each other in the constituency of Trois-Rivieres, or in the constituency of Saint-Maurice, of Champlain, in the 04 area, was through the media. But after 1984, teamwork became possible. No matter who is an MLA, no matter who is an MP, people work as a team. And that is important in my view. That is how a region, a province, a country will grow.
Let us look at what is provided for in the Meech Lake Accord. First, the two official languages are recognized. I think that goes without saying. Second, Quebec's distinct nature is recognized. For the reasons I indicated, this again
October 19, 1987

follows as reasonable. Third, appointments to the Senate and the Supreme Court are made with the concurrence, at the suggestion of the provinces. You know, Madam Speaker, if appointments to the Senate had been made with the concurrence and at the suggestion of the provinces these past 10 years, we might not in 1987 be stymied by the Senate on such a piece of legislation as Bill C-22. And you read today, in both Le Devoir and La Presse, a page sponsored by the Coalition in Support of Bill C-22 on Drugs, which listed the Senators who supported the Bill and those who opposed it or abstained.
It is intolerable for example to see that the Senator representing our region, Mr. Maurice Riel, abstained or did not vote on an issue that will bring 1,500 new jobs apd investments of $600 million to Metropolitan Montreal. Had Quebec Senators been nominated by the Governement of Quebec, had they been willing to do their duty, that is to defend their province's interests, these Senators would have been on their knees to vote in favour of Bill C-22 which will bring to Montreal and to the whole province major investments and many new jobs.
Madam Speaker, once more this shows the importance of the Meech Lake Accord. Because the major role of the Senate and Senators, a role that is theirs since 1867, is not a partisan one. Their major duty is to protect the interests of the province they represent in the Senate.
That was their role in 1867. And here they are in 1987 trying to prevent the passage of bills that are important to a province and to the country as a whole.
So I hope that with the Meech Lake Accord, we will find ourselves in a position where, in the medium term naturally, the Senate will play its proper role and the 10 provinces will work in co-operation with the federal Government, as they have been doing since 1984, for the advancement and the welfare of the whole country as well as every region.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, I want to ask all Members of this House to vote in favour of the Meech Lake Accord. Let nobody come to us to explain the theories or the principles of 1960. This is 1987 and in 1987, we owe it to ourselves to look at the reality of Quebec, the reality of the Maritimes, the reality of Ontario, of the West and of British Columbia. If we consider everything, if we look at all the people who govern this country and who agree on the Meech Lake Accord, I think we owe it to ourselves to vote yes. My dream, Madam Speaker, would be to see this House vote unanimously in favour of the Accord.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions or comments? Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Westmoreland-Kent (Mr. Robichaud).

Madam Speaker, I wish to thank you for this opportunity to speak on this Accord and to participate in this debate which, like Hon. Members who spoke before me, I consider to be historic.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
It goes without saying that we are discussing our country's most fundamental law, a law which is the basis for the drafting and interpretation of all other laws.
But I am rising today, Madam Speaker, first to support the amendments proposed by my Leader. I support them first because they will bring more clarity, they will improve the text and will include in the Constitution some groups of our society that were left out.
It is a pity because this is a historic Accord and, as I mentioned earlier, this is a historic moment and we should not leave out certain groups or certain Canadian men and women. And, Madam Speaker, this is why I find it very important to amend the Meech Lake Accord as we are suggesting.
As most Canadians, if not all of them, I am glad to see what this Accord is trying to do for Quebecers. We hear people saying that at last, the Province of Quebec is coming back to the Constitutional fold. It had to be so. In fact, I am one of those who believe that Quebec has never been away from the Canadian family. 1 think that throughout our history, throughout the debates which were held in this House, and in all federal-provincial agreements, the Province of Quebec was present and I think that Quebecers and Quebec representatives have made their views known and exercized all their rights and privileges as Canadian citizens.
The Province of Quebec is recognized as a distinct society in the first paragraph of the Accord. This clause does not raise any problem inasmuch as it doesn't take anything away from other groups forming the Canadian society.
The distinctiveness of a society is attributable to its culture, its morals, its language, its customs and, of course, its history. So, the term "distinct society", could be applied to many other Canadian groups.
As we are talking about the distinct society concept, we might refer to Acadia, as I believe that we, Acadians, might also be called a distinct society. We have our customs and, as you will certainly recognize, Madam Speaker, we also have our history, part of which has been rather turbulent. Acadians did everything they could to remain Canadians, and even though we have been deported from Acadia at a certain period in our history, we finally came back. We came back here to stay. And of course, we are happy to be part of Canada.
Our territory does not follow provincial borders as Acadians are scattered all over the Atlantic Region. They are mostly concentrated in New Brunswick, but there are Acadians in Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and even all along the eastern coast of the United States.
So, we can say that we have our own history, our own customs and, of course, our own language, even though we are told that we speak with an accent.

October 19, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
It is precisely because of that, Madam Speaker, that we have our own language and regional terms. We, Acadians, could therefore claim as a group the right to be called a distinct society, but I would simply like the existence of this group to be recognized, just as the existence of other groups, such as our native people, to name but one. It is precisely because of this that we have proposed the following in paragraphs 1(c) and 1(d) of our first amendment:
(c)	the recognition that aboriginal peoples constitute a distinctive and fundamental characteristic of Canada;
(d)	the recognition of the multicultural nature of Canadian society, and in particular respect for the many origins, creeds and cultures as well as the differing regional identities that helped shape Canadian society;
I believe that we could all agree on this amendment as it recognizes the existence of the various groups which make up the great Canadian family.
I would also like the House to support the second amendment, which states the following:
"2(a) The role of the Parliament of Canada to preserve and promote, and the role of the provincial legislatures to preserve and, subject to subparagraph (2)(b) to promote, the fundamental characteristic of Canada referred to in paragraph 1(a) is affirmed.
Madam Speaker, it is very important for the Parliament of Canada to play this role of promoting minority groups. Simple protection is not enough; these groups must also be promoted.
New Brunswick has been recognized since 1982 as a bilingual province where French and English have the same status in all matters related to the Government of New Brunswick. The province has therefore been officially bilingual for five years. However, Madam Speaker, there is still a lot to be done. When you call various government agencies, you cannot always get an answer in French. Naturally, progress has been made, but it has been slow and I hope that the new McKenna Government will be able to accelerate the process of making government agencies totally bilingual.
As concerns the promotion of minorities, I shall refer to past experience in New Brunswick, where groups of Acadians were assumed to have been assimilated for all practical purposes because the authorities had been satisfied to protect these groups and to maintain the status quo. Well, to a minority mere protection means assimilation. And those communities which I mentioned earlier, which for all practical purposes were thought to have been assimilated, finally woke up one day and are now in very good health. They are doing very well. Why? Because it was decided that someone should promote this Acadian culture, this group which is known as the New Brunswick Acadians. These people were provided with meeting centres where they could gather for entertainment, sharing common experiences, devising new ways to stick together and develop this culture which was thought to have been lost. This kind of promotion made it possible for these people to wake up, even though these groups were in New Brunswick, Canada's only bilingual province.
So I am firmly convinced, Madam Speaker, that it is very important for Canadian Parliament to assume responsibility not only for protecting minority groups but also for promoting them.
Now we are being told that the Meech Lake Accord is Quebec's turn. Well, I have nothing against that, but my question is this: When will we Acadians have our turn? When will native people and multicultural groups have theirs? I would suggest we ought to take the opportunity we now have to include in Quebec's turn the other groups who feel left out. And I do not believe this Accord is all that fragile, nor that it will quite simply fall apart if it is amended. As a matter of fact, the amendments we are proposing are intended to improve the Accord, to make it clearer, to change the Meech Lake Accord without weakening it, as my colleague has suggested.
In the time allotted to me, which happens to be drawing to a close, I should like to talk about fisheries, which have been included in the Accord. Madam Speaker, I am somewhat concerned over the fact that fisheries will be on the agenda of all future First Ministers' conferences. Fisheries conferences have been constitutionalized. Not so very long ago 1 heard my colleague say it was quite terrible to see that the Conservative Government was prepared to slap a tax on our bread and our butter. I believe all Hon. Members agree that a tax on bread and butter is something for which Canadians will probably not stand still. Putting fisheries on the agenda of all future federal-provincial conferences dealing with constitutional issues is tantamount to putting our bread and butter on the table and taking a chance that somebody might appropriate them.
For us fisheries are very important. In New Brunswick we have some 6,500 fishermen providing work for some 13,000 people on shore in some 125 fish processing plants. Fisheries are of prime importance to us.
How can you explain that it was deemed necessary and advisable to put fisheries on the table. I suppose, Madam Speaker, that they must have been included in the last instance to accommodate someone who was intent on grabbing the jurisdiction on fisheries. This is completely unacceptable for the people of New Brunswick. It is utterly unacceptable!
Madam Speaker, I would go as far as supporting the amendment put forward by my leader who wants that the roles and responsibilities concerning fisheries be put on the agenda for the first meeting only. As a matter of fact, if the subject of fishery is to come up at every meeting, a degree of instability will mar the fishing industry which will certainly not help the people from the Atlantic provinces and those from New Brunswick in particular.
Madam Speaker, I feel strongly about this amendment. You are indicating to me that my time is almost up and that I have just about one minute left.
October 19, 1987

In closing, 1 will talk about a majority group, because up to now I have only dealt with minority groups. This majority group that feels threatened, that feels its rights to equality might have been impaired, is the women's group. We need an amendment to make sure that under this Accord their right to equality will not be curtailed.
Madam Speaker, I take this opportunity to read a few lines from the letter I received from the New Brunswick Advisory Council on the Status of Women: "The Advisory Council supports the amendments to the Meech Lake Accord that will ensure that women's rights to equality will not be reduced".
In fact, that is exactly the purpose of our last amendment which ensures that the Constitution Act of 1987 doesn't allow derogation to the rights and freedoms guaranteed in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Madam Speaker, I will vote in favour of the amendments and I ask all Hon. Members to take a good look at them and to make sure that they don't weaken in any way the Meech Lake Accord.

Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague representing New Brunswick and, to a certain extent, the French community outside Quebec, for his speech. 1 can hardly understand what deep motivations induced him to such a decision. Without any hesitation whatsoever, he reopened that Accord notwithstanding the fact that if a community could pretend to be the first founding community of this nation, it is the Acadian community. But more than any other group, the Acadian community has been literally decimated by the culture shock of the surrounding English-speaking population. Nevertheless, there is still a vibrant community in New Brunswick, a province that has recognized our two official languages. Nova Scotia has not done so, even though it is the land of the first bastion of Louisbourg. I have a hard time understanding the deep motives of our colleague who is definitely against the Accord and accuses us of providing minorities with crutches because-
Not at all!
I am not talking about you but about one of your colleagues in your party.

I am sorry ... It is Laurier. I thank my hon. colleague.
He says that we are providing crutches for minorities. He should remember the astounding rate of assimilation and loss of culture. I am not talking about the bilingualism ratio, for I think it will be an ever more pressing need in our communities to have more and more bilingualism. What I am concerned about here is your community, and I am sorry that you would want to resort to excuses that are nothing more than excuses
Constitution Amendment, 1987
and that did not stand under the scrutiny of the Joint Committee on the Constitution .. .
When you were talking about women's rights being threatened, this has not been proven by anyone in any way. When you talk about promotion of your cultural reality, of your distinct society, you know very well-and in your own province; I am not sure Mr. McKenna is willing to recognize your distinct society because he is not prepared apparently to recognize this wonderful agreement which enables the great Canadian family to reunify. When you stated in your speech, my dear colleague, that you never-

I was thinking about what are, in my opinion, unfounded affirmations. Do not forget that, in 1980, the situation was serious, this country almost split in two. I am just as concerned as you are. Even the committee made some recommandations. It went as far as preparing the agendas for the next constitutional conferences. Your desire to solve everything might jeopardize what we already have. That is the problem.
You are an Acadian, I let you react to that. Madam Speaker, I let my colleague reply to these thoughts.

Madam Speaker, I realize the Accord is dear to the heart of the Hon. Member for Charlevoix (Mr. Hamelin), and I respect the Hon. Member's opinion. He says I made gratuitous statements to the effect that women were threatened, but that is not what I said. I said that certain groups felt threatened. And that is precisely the case with

October 19, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
women. They feel their equality rights are being threatened. I am sure that was not the intention of the provincial Premiers and the Prime Minister of Canada. It was certainly not their intention, but the fact remains that this majority component of our society feels threatened. And I believe it would be appropriate for us to make the requisite changes here in the House so that this group can feel comfortable with the Constitution and with this Constitutional Accord. And what you said about Mr. McKenna, that he might-
What he said.

Excuse me, Madam Speaker. The Hon. Member said that Mr. McKenna might cause the Accord to fall apart, and I may recall what Mr. McKenna said when he appeared before the committee, and 1 quote:
My belief is that those changes must fundamentally represent two factors. One of those criteria is that it must not nullify the principles agreed to in the Langevin Accord. Secondly, any amendments should further advance or clarify the rights of Canadians.
So 1 do not see why the Hon. Member feels threatened and feels the Accord is threatened, to the point of saying that the Accord may fall apart. Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest to the Hon. Member's speech, and of course, his concerns about womens' rights and the historic Langevin Accord. speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy).

Madam Speaker, I have a number of comments to make on the Meech Lake Accord. I intend to vote for it with members of my Party because we feel it does in fact put in concrete terms the commitment that many Canadians from outside of Quebec made to the Province of Quebec and to Quebecois at the time of the referendum seven years ago. At that time I was in the Ontario Legislature as Leader of my Party and I remember that we all spoke in the debate at that time saying to Quebec and Quebecers: "Please do not vote to take your province out of Canada". We asked Quebecers to stay within Canada and we made a commitment.
I was at the provincial level at that time, but the people in Parliament also made a commitment as well as Canadians from coast to coast, that this country would be different and the conditions which had led Quebecers to consider they might want to separate from Canada would be addressed and resolved, not at some infinite point in the future but as a matter of urgency.
For a time I think there was a real risk and danger that that commitment would become forgotten. I am proud now to take part in a debate where we in the Parliament of Canada, now that I am a Member of Parliament, can participate in the historic event that Quebec and Quebecers are able to say yes to Confederation and, yes, to the rest of Canada as the rest of Canada says yes to Quebec. It is about time this took place. Frankly, I think any Member of Parliament who decides to hang back saying: "It is not quite right, it is not quite the time", is guilty of ignoring just what this historic achievement means and of not understanding that the time is now. We have to honour the commitment made to Quebec at the beginning of this decade.
October 19, 1987

Of all the sections in the Meech Lake Accord, the most important sections, I believe, are those that speak directly to the agenda, which was effectively set by Premier Levesque and reiterated in a somewhat different form by Premier Bourassa over the course of the middle of the 1980s. There is a response. At last the Constitution of Canada will say what New Democrats have said it should say for many years. From the time of the foundation of my Party back in 1961, we have said that Canada and Canadians must recognize that Quebec is a distinct society. We have tried to say it in different ways, and at times we have been strongly criticized for it, just as the former Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party was strongly criticized in the 1960s when he argued for acceptance of the deux nations that existed in Canada at that time and exists to this day.
We now have in the Constitution, in the Meech Lake Accord, the recognition that the existence of French-speaking Canadians centred in Quebec but present elsewhere in Canada, and English-speaking Canadians concentrated outside of Quebec but also present in Quebec, constitutes a fundamental characteristic of Canada, and the recognition that Quebec constitutes within Canada a distinct society. All of the implications of what that means have yet to be spelled out in terms of how the Supreme Court, as the arbitrator of our Constitution, approaches this particular question, but we finally had the courage to say to Quebec: "Yes, Quebec is a distinct society because of the language and culture which is French". This is something so fundamental to the nature of Canada that it must be recognized in the Constitution itself.
Elsewhere-and I will come to that today and possibly when this debate resumes in a day or two-there are the other points that speak directly to the concerns of Quebec, particularly that Quebec have a veto over matters that are primordial and fundamental to the existence of provincial powers in Quebec, and that Quebec have the right to opt out of any transfers of provincial powers to the federal Government.

Madam Speaker, I was a member of the Quebec Committee of my Party for a two year period, after which we finally succeeded in preparing a policy statement of the New Democratic Party which received virtually unanimous support at our national Convention in Montreal in March of 1987.
This policy statement was a resolution on Quebec and the Constitution on which we worked together. We worked on the basis of equality. The Quebec Committee of our Party was made up of eight members, led by our party Leader, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent).
Madam Speaker, this group was working on a historic statement since it would be the first convention of our party held in Montreal.
I would like to read to the House the formula proposed by our Party. We were able to compare it in March with the formula agreed to by the Prime Minister at Meech Lake,
Constitution Amendment, 1987
which is now part of the constitution and our statutes thanks to the Meech Lake Accord.
We began by several whereas clauses:
Whereas Quebec must be invited to fashion with the rest of Canada a renewed Federation devoted to cultural and economic equality; and
Whereas the people of Quebec have the right to determine freely their own future; and
Whereas Quebec is unique by the fact that it is the only province where French is the language and culture of the majority; and
Whereas such a specificity obviously implies that Quebecers will continue to fashion their economic, social, cultural and linguistic future by means which could be different from those of the other provinces; and
Whereas this unique character is an asset not only for Quebecers, but also for all other Canadians.
While offering an opening to examine other constitutional amendments, it is therefore resolved by the New Democratic Party that:
1.	The preamble of the Canadian Constitution recognize the unique character of Quebec, the only province where French is the language and culture of the majority;
2.	Quebec must be able to preserve its distinct identity and that one of the means to reach that goal be the right not to participate in constitutional amendments that would lead to a transfer of provincial powers to the federal government and that, when those constitutional amendments have a financial impact, Quebec be entitled to an equivalent financial compensation;
3.	that Quebec have a veto on any constitutional amendment that would alter federal institutions when those changes are considered as vital for the protection and safeguard of the French language and culture in Quebec;
4.	Be it further resolved that the Quebec Committee of the federal NDP explore new constitutional provisions both to preserve the language rights of the majority in Quebec and to maintain the language rights that minorities presently enjoy in the Constitution.
Madam Speaker, I see that my time is over and I would like to make further comments on that resolution which was passed almost unanimously by our Convention, last March, and to compare how that Statement of principles of the New Democratic Party was included in the Statement of principles agreed to by the Prime Minister and the Premiers in the Meech Lake and Langevin Agreements signed last spring.
I hope to conclude my speech when the debate resumes in one or two days.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stan J. Hovdebo (Prince Albert) moved
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   AUDITOR GENERAL ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-262, an Act to amend the Auditor General Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Madam Speaker, in a month from now I will have been a member of the Public Accounts Committee for eight years. During that period of time the committee has often been frustrated by the time it takes for issues which the Auditor General finds in his comprehensive audits of Departments of the Government to be completed and the time it takes before they can be put before the Public Accounts Committee and Parliament.
I must say that I was exceedingly disappointed when the committee responsible for making the decision as to whether this Bill was votable or not decided it was not of great enough importance to be called a votable Bill. This Bill, or facsimiles of it, have been before the House three times before. In each case the Government has agreed that action should be taken, but in the end either time ran out or the opportunity for
changes to the Auditor General Act were not able to go forward.
A meeting of the Public Accounts Committee was held on May 28, 1984, at which the Auditor General made a statement which I think should be before this House. He said that the Auditor General's office had studied the pros and cons of the reporting system and that he had come up with what he thought was an acceptable procedure, and with very small changes in the Auditor General Act it could be put into effect. He said, "We settled on completion-date for reporting plus a short summary annual report as the best and most flexible alternative". In other words, his office made the recommendation that it would be better for the office of the Auditor General if it could make the report after it had completed the comprehensive audit, as short a time afterwards as possible, allowing only for printing time, and then table it with the Speaker who would in turn table it in the House. As you well know, Madam Speaker, the Speaker has a continuing commitment to refer any Auditor General's report to the Public Accounts Committee.
On June 13 of 1984 the Public Accounts Committee made this statement:
Your committee considered the reporting practices of the Auditor General and in particular the timeliness of his annual report to the House of Commons. Your committee notes that under the present Auditor General Act the Auditor General normally may report only annually to the House of Commons. Your committee favours the reporting of comprehensive and other audits on a completion-date basis. This will enable your committee to deal with the Auditor General's finding in a timely manner and to exert its remedial influences as soon as possible after the audit is completed. The Auditor General endorses this approach because it provides for greater efficiency and flexibility in his reporting to Parliament.
That was the request of the Public Accounts Committee on June 13, 1984.
The amendment that I am suggesting here in this Bill is very simple. As I said, it has been reported by every Public Accounts Committee since 1979. It has been before this House three times and it has been accepted by members of the Opposition and government Members. It is not a votable Bill at the moment. However, the House has the opportunity and the authority to let this Bill, before the end of this hour of debate, go to committee. If the political will is here it can go to committee and what actions should be taken on it can be discussed at that time.
There was an agreement in about 1980 or 1981 with the previous administration to allow-and the wording was even decided upon at that time-the amendments to go through to become part of a changed Auditor General Act. In 1985, to assist in the speed up of the report of the Auditor General, we asked and agreed with the Auditor General that the report be presented in October instead of December, thus allowing a couple of months for attention to be given to it by the Public Accounts Committee in the year that the report was tabled instead of waiting until after the Christmas break.
October 19, 1987

In the meeting I was discussing on May 29, 1984, the Public Accounts Committee spent a considerable amount of time discussing the pros and cons and the resulting change to the legislation. There was entire agreement at that time on what would be required in this Bill.
The Bill is very simple and straightforward. It has three very small changes. The major change was adding the words "at least". The Bill states:
7.(1) The Auditor General shall report at least annually to the House of Commons
(a)	on the work of his office; and
(b)	on whether, in carrying on the work of his office, he received all the information and explanations he required.
There are two subsequent clause changes, one ensuring that any report brought before the House or given to the Speaker is laid before the House; and a third clause which takes into consideration that this change has been made in the Act.
A very short change in the Act would give Parliament considerably more opportunity to deal with the Public Accounts of Canada and the Auditor General's report.
The pros and cons when discussed by the Standing Committee on Public Accounts brought it to the decision that what was required was a change in this legislation. The wording that I have put into the Bill is exactly the same as the words suggested by the Public Accounts Committee.
The Bill was presented to the House on October 21, 1985. At that time several Members of the House, both on the government and on the opposition side, commented on the need for the Bill to be passed. Members brought forward many cases in which, had this Bill been in place, we may have been able to save the Government and the people of Canada many millions of dollars. On October 21, 1985 such examples were given as the case of Canadair which cost the Government approximately $3.8 billion. A considerable amount of that money may have been saved had the structure under which Canadair was operating been brought to the Public Accounts Committee and the attention of Parliament eight or twelve months before when the comprehensive account had been finished. Also at that time the Hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) mentioned the case of the scientific research credit which cost the people of Canada approximately $2 billion before it was entirely stopped. Had that situation been brought before the Public Accounts Committee at an earlier time, we may have been able to save part of that money.
On Tuesday, October 27, the Auditor General's report will be tabled in the House. It is possible and likely that some of the audits in that report could have been completed or may have been completed in August of 1986, which is 14 months ago. By now the Public Accounts Committee and Parliament could have dealt with any of the shortcomings brought to light by the Auditor General in that report. In his 1984 report the Auditor General made the following statement:
Auditor General Act
The fiscal year on which i am only now reporting concluded eight months
ago. it will be several more months before the Public Accounts Committee
(PAC) will have completed its consideration of this Report. I am anxious to
see the whole process speeded up.
If one were to look at the evidence of that particular meeting when we discussed that report, it would be found that the Auditor General also indicated that some of the reports completed eight months before, or that were brought to the Public Accounts Committee eight months before, had actually been completed almost one year before that. This meant that some of the reports were two years old by the time they came to the Public Accounts Committee.
This amendment will not change any of the powers of the Auditor General or the Public Accounts Committee. It will change no powers and have no effect on the Parliament of Canada. It will increase the flexibility and the ability of Parliament to deal with those comprehensive audits.
There are three very good reasons why Parliament should pass this Bill, and it has the power to do so today by sending it to committee. It would be better for Parliament because it would always be working on more up-to-date material. It would be better for the Government because it would have a quicker analysis of the programs which have been analysed by the Auditor General.
In the report of the Auditor General of May 29, 1985 he also indicated that not only would it be very helpful to have those reports examined earlier, but that it would also be much more cost effective. Instead of holding those reports and going over them, they would be submitted in smaller booklets. The Auditor General would also continue to publish an annual report which would report on those items which are not necessarily directly connected to a comprehensive audit.
I call upon Parliament, both opposition and government Members, to accept this Bill and send it to committee in order that it can be looked at and the committee can decide whether it wishes to take the action to allow those changes to the Auditor General Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude Lanthier (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   AUDITOR GENERAL ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I accepted to take part in this debate on Bill C-262, sponsored by my hon. colleague, the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo).
At first glance, what is most striking about this Bill is its simplicity and particularly the obvious desire of the Hon. Member for Prince Albert to ensure a better control of public finances through more frequent reports from the Auditor General.
It is not the first time that this Bill is tabled as it has been already debated in 1985 when it was introduced as Bill C-250.
I do not think that any Member will question the absolute necessity of a continuing and quasi-immediate control on Government's spending. In fact, it may seem difficult to study

October 19, 1987
Auditor General Act
financial statements that are 18 to 24 months old and to correct adequately the problems brought to light.
Obviously, the financial disease which is sapping the strength of the Departments ana Crown corporations concerned could kill them by causing a haemorrhage of funds before we have time to react adequately.
With the proposed amendment, it would become possible to bring more rapidly to the attention of parliamentarians urgent matters requiring pressing or immediate solutions. So, the Auditor General might present, and I quote, an important provisiqn of the Bill: "A special report to the House of Commons on any matter of pressing importance or urgency that, in his opinion, should be reported immediately."
The nuance between the present legislation and the bill is subtle, although it does emphasize the need to react immediately without waiting for the annual report on activities of the relevant Department or Crown corporation.
Nevertheless, it seems to me that the Bill, with its present provisions, could lead to some abuse. But it would be possible for the Public Accounts Committee to request, or even demand, special studies on some Departments on the basis of rumours or hearsay, and God knows how much the Opposition likes this kind of thing. The process would be slowed down if too many requests were directed to the Auditor General. His office does not have unlimited resources to undertake numerous special studies while meeting deadlines on its main current assignments, which are to audit financial statements from Departments and Crown corporations. The Auditor General should not be rendered unable to fulfil his primary mandate due to the fact that the Standing Committee on Public Accounts would impose an overburden of secondary responsibilities based, as I said before, on rumour or intentions which are of dubious value even at first glance.
One other drawback has to do with the possibility of partisan politics. Here again, some colleagues thrive on that aspect of our parliamentary life. As it stands now, the bill does not place any restrictions or propose any guidelines with regard to the circumstances which would justify a special study. As the bill now stands, it seems to me that the Standing Committee on Public Accounts could base on any motive whatsoever a request that an inquiry be made by the Auditor General. Unfortunately, we are therefore faced with the possibility that such requests would be made on a purely partisan basis, and this is totally unacceptable.
To maintain its reputation of non partisanship, the Public Accounts Committee must never find itself in situations likely to give rise to accusations of partisanship that would weaken its efficiency. Unhappily, the Bill does not protect it in that respect. Having said this, changes such as these are imperative. We all know of situations that are brought about due to the weakness of the present system. Although the Auditor may find disturbing situations in some Departments and inform these consequently, the present system is such that even after the Auditor General's report has been published and is examined by the Committee, that is 18 to 24 months after the
problem has been disclosed, Departments may still not be able to take corrective action.
Madam Speaker, it would be inappropriate to ask this House to amend an Act which is working smoothly if the amendments bear no solutions. As proposed now, they only emphasize problems. Have you ever seen for instance an enterprise, except maybe for those who make the headlines because of their serious financial difficulties, wait from 18 to 24 months after the end of a fiscal year to examine the documents of an auditor? No; this is however the way the Government of Canada manages public moneys, Madam Speaker. This is a serious deficiency which we can all see, unfortunately.
To remedy this problem, the control should come back at the level where the founders of Canada put it in the first place, namely to Parliament and to elected representatives.
When I refer to elected representatives, I want to make the distinction in relation to the other place.
In 1984, Canadians elected their Members of Parliament so that they put some order in the public finances. It is good to see that Bills try effectively to remedy problems and to restore a fair balance. During the last election campaign, Madam Speaker, I recall visiting a garage owner in my area well known for his blunt language and his sound management. He asked me if I had ever been in politics, and I answered that no, unfortunately, I had only a background of business and industrial administration. He told me: "That's exactly what we need. Go to Ottawa and tell the federal people to stop trying to show us how to run our business like a government, and show them how to run a government like a business." Madam Speaker, I suggest that the principle of the law should be kept in this edited section of the Bill, but since it has been introduced by people who are not particularly noted for their business acumen, I mean our socialist colleagues in the House, we should not expect this consideration to be directly affected by the Bill before us.
Madam Speaker, we have been specifically mandated to keep a close watch on federal expenditures and administration and to reduce the deficit which was threatening the growth of our economy, and even seriously mortgaging that of future generations of Canadians. We must therefore take steps which will meet the expectations of Canadians for a better control of our basic public moneys.
In order to achieve our objective and fulfil our mandate, however, we must take the necessary step to identify and eliminate the sources of waste. The responsibility of our Auditor General is to show us where situations exist which might develop into serious problems. He must keep a close watch over public accounts, but because his hands are tied he might not react with enough flexibility and quickness to fulfil his mandate. If he cannot do a good job, we will not be able to assume our responsibility of monitoring public expenditures with precision and effectiveness.
October 19, 1987

That is the reason why the Bill before us is interesting. Perfectly aware of the possible shortcomings of the current financial control system of the Government, of the comments made by newspaper columnists, as well as the great many letters to the editor coming from our concerned citizens, I feel that the time has come to take the difficult but necesesary steps which are certainly needed. Squandering the taxpayer's money must come to an end. This squandering added to outright losses of money, results in further losses that are considerably more difficult to quantify. Plow can we assign a monetary value to some of our fellow citizens losing confidence in our parliamentary process, for instance? How can we assign a monetary value to Canadian and foreign investors losing confidence, and becoming reluctant to go ahead and establish or expand their business, after having been previously threatened with seizure by one Party or with nationalization by another?
Madam Speaker, all those considerations deserve very special attention in this debate, because they, combined with the domino effect resulting from the financial mismanagement of the nation's affairs, have an impact on all other fields of activity, whether social, economic or political, in our country.
1 therefore urge this Governement to question the reason for that process. We certainly must act before it is too late. We all remember the former Auditor General, Mr. Maxwell Henderson, saying that the Government was losing control over public expenditures. It was time indeed that we came to power and brought this control back to a strong and well-balanced business-minded House of Commons. We have gone a long way since then, but there is still a lot to be done. The Bill now before us is a step forward along the road to nationalization- sorry, "rationalizaton", tongues keep slipping when something is suggested by the Socialist Party-the rationalization of public expenditures. But I am not convinced this is enough. I therefore urge the Government to stop and think the matter over. We must ask ourselves whether everything has been done in that area. Sincerely, I do not believe so. We must also see what additional measures are needed to improve on our financial management.
Madam Speaker, this Government has already done much in that area of financial control and Government expenditures. It is my hope it will stay on that road, finding other means, and that it will be guided along the way by proposals and suggestions such as the one outlined in this Bill. However, we must recognize it is still inadequate and incomplete.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   AUDITOR GENERAL ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
If the Hon. Member for LaSalle wrote that speech, I advise him to do a little more research from now on and to get better informed because what he said in the House, Madam Speaker, does not hold if you consider that people who usually have much more clout than he in this House have already considered and solved that matter by saying to the Government: Yes, we must give the Auditor General the opportunity to bring forward more than one report. It is, I think, a blunt answer coming not only from some Members but from the Auditor General and, as I said earlier, from the Minister himself, the present Minister of State (Treasury Board) (Mr. Lewis) who used to be Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee... The Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), who presently chairs the Public Accounts Committee, also supported that resolution. The Hon. Member seems to have suddenly decided that he had to speak against this initiative.
Madam Speaker, we have positive comments to make on that issue. I think that Bill C-262 should be passed as it will give to the Auditor General the opportunity to provide the House with the tools it requires to do its job. The AG is senior official of the House. He takes no orders from anyone. He takes no orders from Hon. Members and even less from the Hon. Member for LaSalle. He takes no orders from committees nor the House because his powers have been given to him by the House and parliamentarians.
I fail to understand how it can be alleged that a special study could be requested for purely partisan reasons.
Madam Speaker, that kind of allegation can only be made by someone who does not know the Auditor General's job, who does not understand anything about his role. The Auditor

October 19, 1987
Auditor General Act
General is independent from any political pressure and reports to the House of Commons and, as was said earlier, he will report next week by tabling a rather bulky report. Last year, it weighed about one and a quarter or one and half pounds and contained more than 500 pages. The committee must study the report, and Bill C-262 only suggests that the Auditor General be allowed to report to the House as soon as he finishes a study on any subject, contrary to what the interpretation of the Act authorizes him to do presently.
Let us come back to Bill C-262. It proposes to amend Sections 7 and 8.
Subsection 7(1) at present reads as follows:
7.(1) The Auditor General shall report annually to the House of Commons
(a)	on the work of his office; and
(b)	on whether, in carrying on the work of his office, he received all the
information and explanations he required.
The Hon. Member would like to amend this subsection by adding the two words "at least", so that the new subsection would read:
The Auditor General shall report at least annually to the House of
Commons-
And so on and so forth.
Madam Speaker, the idea would not be to have 25 reports a year. The Office of the Auditor General which I have contacted today has advised me that seven or eight reports might be tabled in the House every year, in addition to the statutory annual report which must be tabled before the end of the year, generally in October. Last year, it was tabled on October 21 and this year it will be tabled next Tuesday, October 27.
Madam Speaker, I think Hon. Members could work much more effectively both in committee and in the House. I think the Office of the Auditor General could operate much more effectively if it were to submit to the House for study and consideration some of the chapters as soon as their review has been completed. By so doing, we would not have to deal as we do now with a bulky annual report in November and December and try to understand the report on various federal departments and agencies and devise concrete and corrective measures to ensure a more efficient and healthier federal administration. That is the role of the Auditor General. All that is being requested is that the House accept of its own will that the Auditor General may make special reports, several times a year if it is warranted in his opinion, in order to spread over a period of time his projects or reports on matters that deserve a more careful study.
Bill C-262 would amend section 8 to provide for reports on matters of urgency. Subsection 8(1) at present reads as follows:
"8. (1) The Auditor General may make a special report to the House of Commons on any matter of pressing importance or urgency that, in his opinion, should not be deferred until the presentation of his annual report
The Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) would like to make the following amendment by deleting the last two lines and substituting the following therefor:
"8. (1) The Auditor General may make a special report to the House of Commons on any matter of pressing importance or urgency that, in his opinion, should be reported immediately."
The purpose of this amendment is not to enable us to react and ask for inquiries, or to have the Auditor General take his orders from Hon. Members or to abuse a system which is essential for this Parliament. We would like to give the Auditor General the power to make regular inquiries and reports and spread his work over a period of time and make a better use of his human resources so that we will be able, in this House, with the help of our committee, to know how this country is run. It is as simple as that, Madam Speaker.
I have a few comments to make on where we stand with this Bill. On July 18, 1980, the Auditor General recommended the use of special reports to the House of Commons and the committee. In 1982 these changes to the Auditor General Act were agreed to by the Public Accounts Committee, the Auditor General himself, the President of the Treasury Board, the House Leader of the Official Opposition and the New Democratic caucus. We all agreed this was an important change and that we should proceed. On June 13, 1984 in its fifth report to Parliament the Public Accounts Committee recommended the reporting of comprehensive and other audits on a completion date basis. When a stage and a report is finished, and an audit has been made, it is reported to the House so we can have access to the report. The fifth report went on to say that this would enable the committee to deal with the Auditor General's findings in a timely manner and to exert its remedial influence as soon as possible after the audit is completed. On March 31, 1984, the Auditor General in his annual report to Parliament, under "matters of special importance and interest" brought to the attention of Parliament the recommendation of the Public Accounts Committee of June 13, 1984 to amend-let me emphasize the words to amend-the Auditor General Act to allow for completion date reporting by his office.
I cannot put it any better than that. We had a debate in this House a year or two ago on the same question. I want to congratulate the mover of this Bill because I think it is an important one. I hope the House will see fit to pass it and get it into committee so we can get a proper amendment before us and proceed with what I think is a very constructive and positive effort on the part of the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   AUDITOR GENERAL ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to rise in Private Members' Hour to deal with a very important subject. The Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) is to be commended for raising it at this time. I share with him a similar set of eight year experiences.
October 19, 1987

Most of my time in this House I have had a passion for the Public Accounts Committee and the work that it does. Other responsibilities, however, from time to time have not allowed the degree of involvement I would have preferred to have had. It ties up with my background as an academic.
I think we in this House do have a strong obligation, each and every one us, to be conscious of the spending patterns of Government, of the need to make sure that the votes we take in this House and the direction we give to the Public Service of Canada about how to spend the money and which programs to spend it on are followed in a legal manner but also in a cost-efficient and effective manner. By bringing forward a Private Member's Bill, the Hon. Member for Prince Albert is, as other speakers have noted, advancing a cause which the Public Accounts Committee itself has historically advanced and one which the Auditor General has advanced since 1982.
I personally have some trouble with the notion of a series of reports. If that series of reports grows to the point at which every three weeks we get another one, I have fears about how that will be seen, unless we make some amendments on Parliament's side of the fence, and that may indeed be possible in the future.
If we move away from the notion of an annual Auditor General's report and to very common, frequent reporting, what will happen? As a Member of the House who from time to time has difficulty communicating with the general public about the Government of Canada, what it is doing right and what it is doing wrong, I must ask myself if we would lose something that is inherent in the public relations aspect of a major report coming down once a year.
The next question I must ask myself is if these reports are coming along, as the Hon. Member just said, on a completion date basis, what does that do to the committee itself? One of the real joys that I experienced as a new Member of Parliament when I was the Vice-Chairman of the committee and the Hon. Member from Westmount was the Chairman in 1979 was to discover a committee of Parliament that was nonpartisan in nature and very consistently so. Members of all political persuasions shared the common goal of wanting to make public expenditures more efficient, effective and cost productive.
Every time an Auditor General's report comes out, there are press conferences and the Auditor General is called as a witness before the committee. The report is explored over two or three sessions so we get the flavour of what the Auditor General has discovered in the previous 12 months about the way the Government of Canada spends money and his feelings about the major areas where change might indeed be needed.
It has been the pattern of the committee to set up a year's worth of work in advance, to say: "Out of this collection of departmental reports and comprehensive audits, what is the committee's judgment about what should be the first topic the
Auditor General Act
committee should tackle and what should be the second and the third and so on; what preparation do we as a committee need for holding hearings, for directing the researchers of the committee to prepare background material for members and for seeking out the proper set of witnesses; and what kind of timeframes are involved?"
I have always gotten a great deal of satisfaction out of that particular committee, in part because of the planned nature of the work. We are able, after the first week or two when the report is first laid on the table, to work quietly and efficiently as a committee without the kind of glare that very often comes from particular committee examinations. I thought that that helped the judgment of committee members. It has been an important part of why the activities of Public Accounts have been less partisan than some of the things I have experienced on the Labour, Employment and Immigration Committee.
If we are topical, there is a tendency to be political. We have an obligation to our own Parties, when there is lots of press about an issue, to advance the causes to which Members have collectively agreed. I think that that is appropriate for 90 per cent to 95 per cent of what we do in this Chamber. However, in the Public Accounts Committee, we are trying to get at the fundamental nature of the Government of Canada. It conducts not so much an examination of decisions made by politicians, by the Government of the day, by the Cabinet of the day, by the majority Party of the day, as it conducts an examination of how the servants of the people of Canada who work in the Public Service conduct the affairs of the nation relating to the instructions which we give them through legislation or policy pronouncements.
Would it be right for that committee to be hopping hither and yon, a day here, a day there and four days over there, simply because there is a constant stream of reports coming before it on different dates at different times? Inevitably, some of those reports would hit the table of the House of Commons when the same subject matter was coincidentally the major topic under discussion the week before in Question Period, or would become for some other set of reasons the major topic in Question Period the week thereafter. Then would we have suspicions that the Auditor General himself was being partisan? Would he all of a sudden be taking advantage of a political event in the country by putting the report on the table at an opportune moment to create maximum publicity?
If we began to worry that this independent office of the Auditor General of Canada was behaving in a partisan political fashion, then I suggest that the very important dimension of independence and non-partisanship which is critically important to the functioning of the office would begin to erode. Over five or 10 years, would it disappear? If it began to look as though the Auditor General was a tool of the Government of the day or a tool of the Opposition of the day, would it then have the kind of impact it deserves and which we so clearly want and need?

October 19, 1987
Auditor General Act
One of the real problems Members of Parliament face on a daily basis is having access to information. We have a Freedom of information Act, and through parliamentary reform, we can investigate, but at the same time there are many laws about the privacy and confidentiality that is a right of Cabinet and a necessary part of cabinet Government.
The Auditor General can follow an information trail from the start right through to the end in a way that the law would not allow Members of Parliament to do. The Auditor General can draw conclusions out of that right which Parliament has given him and thus inform us not so much of the specifics but of the generalities of a problem. If he does that for us on an annual basis in a major report that has high public visibility and high credibility and is sort of enshrined-we all know it is coming at the same time of year-then I think the perception of his independence is clearly enhanced. It would not be the Auditor General's fault that he happened to report on transport at a particular time when the annual report was due if it happened to be a political issue, but if he has the freedom of choice of when to report, there will be a lot more coincidences. Reports will appear in the middle of political upheavals of one kind or another.
If that independence and view of non-partisanship were to disappear, then I think we would be losing something that is critically important to this Chamber.
So I urge Members not so much to reject the argument of the Hon. Member for Prince Albert but to continue this debate. Perhaps there is some middle ground where the Auditor General should be encouraged to use the emergency power he currently has. Not too long ago we felt so strongly about the functioning of this House that we asked him to report as soon as he finished an audit, and he did. It was not part of the annual report but it was brought to this Chamber on a timely basis. Perhaps there could be some clarification so that that happens somewhat more often, but I do not think now is the right time to go this far.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   AUDITOR GENERAL ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have been rather perplexed at the nature of this debate so far. I looked back over my records, notes and files and found that all three political Parties over the last number of years have said that the ideas contained in this Bill are good ideas. The Auditor General has said that this is exactly what he wants to have done. The Standing Committee on Public Accounts has time and time again requested that these things be done. Financial analysts in every part of the country have at one time or another made representations to the Government saying that this is what they require. The economic think-tanks which meet regularly have said on a number of occasions that these are appropriate measures. The present Minister of State for the Treasury Board (Mr. Lewis) said that this was a great idea. I can go on and on listing all sorts of people who have made reasoned arguments in support of these points, but to my surprise, and I suspect that of most of us, when government
Members got up today to speak they said that this is no longer appropriate. "We are going to speak against this Bill." They couched it in nicer terms than that, but the essence was that they are not going to proceed. 1 think I know why.
Every year when the Auditor General files his report there is a flurry in the House and editorials in the papers about how the Government is mismanaging the taxpayers' money. It happens every year and it is rather embarrassing for the Government. It is going to happen again next week. I suspect that what the Government is saying is that it is embarrassed every year because of how it spends taxpayers' money and it does not want to be embarrassed four or five or 10 times a year if the Auditor General were permitted to file reports after he has conducted a comprehensive audit on a government Department or agency.
It seems to me there are two reasons Members of Parliament are elected to form a Government. The first is to collect money from taxpayers in one form or another, and the second is to disburse that money in order to provide services to the taxpayers. One side of this issue is how we collect taxes, but we can leave that debate to another time because we all appreciate that there are many criticisms of that conduct at the moment. However, there are times when the Auditor General ought to have the opportunity to file a report on a particular occurrence if he decides to do so.
Two or three examples come to mind. I remember that not long ago the feeling was that spending in the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion was out of control. It became well known that millions and millions of dollars were not accounted for. The Minister was shifted out of the portfolio and a lot of serious questions were raised. I suspect that the Auditor General should have moved in right there and then and conducted an audit and made his report immediately. That was not done because he can only do so if he determines it to be an emergency. I am not sure how he would do that, but obviously a Minister mismanaging a Department is not an emergency.
Then I remember the furore over the scientific tax credit. Tens of millions of dollars were misappropriated, and I suspect in the end all sorts of criminal charges will be laid against those who misused that program. Again nothing was exposed, but I am sure the Auditor General would have loved to have a look at that.
What this Bill attempts to do is simply to change the Auditor General Act with respect to when it reports to the House of Commons and indirectly to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. Given all the people who have suggested that we do this, I do not see why we do not, if we believe the taxpayer has the right to know how the Government is behaving with taxpayers' money. I think there is a will to do just that. I believe Members of Parliament are anxious to do just that. It would be in the best interests of the country and its taxpayers to allow this Bill by my hon. friend from Prince Albert to go to committee for further examination.
October 19, 1987

I know that my colleague from Ottawa Centre had hoped to make some comments on this Bill today and add his support because he was part of the cry that went out for more accountability so that we as responsible parliamentarians could explain to the people of Canada, our constituents, why the Government is spending money in this or that area and if there is a problem, to identify it quickly.
In the present circumstances, as you will know, by the time the Auditor General gets to a particular audit, it is well along in his year and by the time he reports it might be a year later. By the time the committee gets to it it might be two years out of date. Obviously this is not good enough.
I urge Members of the House to consider this Bill seriously and get on with making this very simple, straightforward change to the Act to allow for more accountability by the Government of Canada.

Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), to ask themselves some other questions. For example, where was he when the Auditor General was reporting during that unbelievable Liberal reign when the Government went from a $7 million deficit to a $180 billion deficit in 1984 when this Government took power? subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   AUDITOR GENERAL ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I am not being political. It is a fact. Clearly this Government has acted on what the Auditor General has said. Regarding initiatives taken towards accountability, and this is not a selected phrase, he said this Government has been accountable to the people of Canada and is moving very swiftly forward. He said that another sign of hope that those responsible for spending taxpayers' dollars were doing so more carefully lies in the increased emphasis on a need for restraint in public expenditures. It is clear that that initiative was taken from the Auditor General's reports of the past. It is clear that the Government is using the Auditor General's report to make decisions on how Canada should govern itself and how it can be prudent with the taxpayers' dollars. For the hon. gentleman to suggest that it report more often is not what is important at this time.
