Madam Speaker, I rise to make some remarks to the House concerning the response to a question I raised in the House a short time ago on behalf of all those who receive the minimum wage for work under federal jurisdiction.
I find it shocking that there is at the present no regular and automatic method for reviewing and increasing the minimum wage in accordance with rises in the cost of living. The people who need the most protection are receiving the least insofar as there has not been in this country, as there is in many others, a way of regularly and automatically reviewing the predicament of those who need the protection of minimum wage legislation and regulation.
The minimum wage for occupations under federal jurisdiction in Canada has not been changed since May, 1986. That may not seem like a long time with regard to certain activities, but it is a long time for people who are trying to make a living on wages as low as $4, the current minimum wage for occupations under federal jurisdiction. That is especially so when we consider that the cost of living, according to the Consumer Price Index, has risen since the last minimum wage increase by 18 cents on $4.
We are asking people to believe and live as though $3.82 can equal $4, for the person earning $4 has purchasing power equal to that of the person who was earning $3.82 when this rate was struck. That is unconscionable. It certainly behoves the Government to take steps to ensure that there will be prompt review in the future and adjustment of the minimum wage in accordance with the cost of living as well as to ensure that this state of affairs is not repeated. Instead, we must replace the present system with one which calls for a periodic review and an adjustment of the minimum wage in accordance with the Consumer Price Index.

October 19, 1987
Adjournment Debate
I am aware of some of the arguments brought against the latter suggestion. I point out that if those arguments are sound they should be directed against the indexation of the Old Age Security pension, the Canada Pension, the pensions of Members of Parliament and the pensions of public servants. In each of those cases I cited there is a quite proper and reasonable indexation of the pensions so that the purchasing power remains constant. No one I have mentioned in any of those pension funds needs the protection more than the person who is working for the minimum wage.
The rationale for a minimum wage which Canada and the provinces have had for approaching half a century is that the people with the least ability to increase their income will nonetheless have that which they must have in order to have a basic human existence. There is no one in this House who would deny any fellow Canadian that. I hope that in raising this matter for the consideration of the House, we will see the seriousness of something which I am sure has been overlooked in competition with other priorities, and that at the earliest possible date there will be steps taken to raise the minimum wage in the federal jurisdiction, bringing it more in line with such minimum wage rates as are now enjoyed by workers labouring under provincial jurisdictions such as the Northwest Territories, $5.00; Manitoba $4.70; Quebec and Ontario, $4.55; Saskatchewan $4.50; the Yukon $4.25. We thus see various jurisdictions in this country which have enacted that their workers must earn more, and will earn more, and I hope we will bring ourselves in line with those jurisdictions and, I hastily add, with the United States, Luxembourg, France and the Netherlands, each of which is now adjusting its minimum wage periodically in accordance with either the cost of living or the prevailing wage rate throughout their countries.

Madam Speaker, first of all, I would like to stress that the Government is proud of the measures taken to protect the purchasing power of workers at the minimum wage since it was elected, and we will remain vigilant in this respect in the future.
The present Government made an in-depth study of its policy on the minimum wage in 1985, after which he announced an increase which brought the minimum wage of adult workers from $3.50 to $4 an hour; this is a 14 percent increase in real terms which came into force on May 26, 1986.
Furthermore, before this review, the minimum wage of workers under 17 was $3.25 an hour, 25 cents or 7 percent below the rate for adults. Since there was a danger that gap might fly in the face of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which prohibits discrimination on account of age, and since this Government remains strongly committed to the principle of equal pay and equal opportunity, we did away with the lower wage rate that applied to the young. The federal minimum wage for workers below 17 years of age was
therefore raised to the adult rate, a significant 23 per cent increase.
The percentages of those two increases, 14 per cent in the case of the minimum wage and 23 per cent for the former youth rate, compare favourably with the 13 per cent increase in the consumer price index since this Government came to power in September of 1984. This last increase in the minimum wage is the first in over six years, since 1981. Currently, the federal minimum wage is more or less at mid-range of the various provincial rates.
This Government takes its role very seriously as regards minimum work standards. In a number of areas, for instance child care leaves, provisions against unfair dismissals, and provisions relating to lay-offs, the Government has assumed leadership. Our minimum wage policy complements our efforts to ensure a basic protection for those workers who are totally or almost totally deprived of negotiating power. That is the thrust of that legislation. We will go on ensuring decent minimum work standards in the interests of all Canadians.
We realize this is not perfect. But I suggest it can be viewed as a step in the right direction.

AGRICULTURE-GRAIN FARMERS-DEFICIENCY PAYMENT/CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE TALKS

Madam Speaker, on October 2 I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) if he was going to make good on a promise he made in late August to western and eastern grain producers to provide some $3 billion in deficiency payments this fall. You will recall, Madam Speaker, that one year ago the Government made a commitment to provide a $1 billion deficiency payment to farmers. That was at the behest of the Premier of Saskatchewan who was locked in a serious provincial election. He called the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) at five o'clock in the morning to get his support for a deficiency payment. This was to rescue him and to provide him with a political bail-out in that election.
Farmers are very concerned right now because the Minister made a commitment, or seemed to have made a commitment in principle, to provide a deficiency payment of some $3 billion. That would include the Western Grain Stabilization Fund payment of about $1 billion. In Question Period on August 2 the Minister seemed to welsh on that deal. He did not give any firm commitment that he would provide it. He talked a great deal about the method of payment, the timing of payment and all the rest of it. But he did not give any commitment.
I also asked the Minister in a supplementary question as to whether the hold up was with regard to the free trade negotiations. In fact, there are two developments in the free trade negotiations which have a great deal to do with the grain
October 19, 1987

industry in this country in that it is very clear now that the two-price system of wheat which provides a $280 million a year benefit to Canadian grain producers will be destroyed by the free trade agreement.
The Minister of Agriculture in Saskatchewan, and the Premier of the province, have owned up to that and have made it clear in the legislature, they have even convinced the federal government to provide a compensation for the loss of the two-price system of wheat. But there is another aspect as well. That is to say that in the agreement the United States undertakes to take "into account", I believe are the exact words, Canada's position with regard to its use of its export enhancement program. That program is essentially designed for the United States to buy markets in Russia, Saudi Arabia and other traditional markets for Canadian wheat producers, but not to exclude the use of that export enhancement program when it gives away one bushel free with every three that are sold. When the Minister said that the delay of the deficiency payment had nothing to do with the free trade negotiations, which were in the final throes at that time, I am not so sure that that was not a consideration.
In any event, western Canadian farmers and eastern farmers feel that they have been sold out by the Government on the free trade deal. They are wondering whether or not the Government will now make good on the deficiency payment of $3 billion which the Minister seemed to agree to in late August in the meeting in Winnipeg.
1 certainly call on the Parliamentary Secretary in his response this afternoon to give a firm commitment that the Government will provide this deficiency payment and that it will not continue to stonewall into the fall months and the winter.

Madam Speaker, when that question was raised last October 2, details had indeed been given to my colleague by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise).
At the meeting held on last August 27, our Government engaged in a consultation process with some 50 Canadian farm leaders to examine the national agricultural situation. Madam Speaker, it was our Government which established that process, that form of consultation with Canadian farmers, it is not. . . and I remind my colleague that recent polls have shown clearly that Canadians highly appreciate the work done by their Agriculture Minister. The satisfaction level is more than 70 per cent.
One of the main points is precisely the consulting attitude of our Government. As the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) recalled on October 2, this was the third meeting with farm leaders as we attempt to find with them ways of cushioning the impact of the continuing world trade subsidy war. The proposal put forward by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is supported by a number of farm groups. We are well
Adjournment Debate
aware of that. If the proposal proves to be fair to all producers and if it proves to be market and production neutral, I think it could form the basis of a new program. Our department officials are now analyzing the proposal along with other possible actions by our Government. We have met CFA staff to discuss the matter and clarify various points. No commitment was given with respect to the dollar value of a program.
The farm leaders themselves estimated about $3 billion would be needed. I do not think the negotiations we have concluded with the United States should be taken as detrimental. They are one element amoung others, but there is no connection with this issue and I think, Madam Speaker, we will keep on meeting the needs of Canadian producers as we have done over the last three years. We will also continue our international activities because everybody is aware, and it is the main concern of our Canadian farmers' friends, that the international trade subsidy war must come to an end. Our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has put agriculture on the agenda of major powers. We will continue our efforts in that sense and I can assure my colleague that Canadian producers will not regret the consultation process we have undertaken with them.
APARTHEID-SOUTH AFRICA-AID TO FRONT-LINE STATES/ECONOM1C SANCTIONS-COMMONWEALTH CONFERENCE

Madam Speaker, I rise today to follow up on a question that I asked in the House on October 13 which had to do with the Commonwealth heads of government conference that was going on at that time in Vancouver. I was concerned to receive assurances from the Government that the emphasis placed on one particular agenda item of the conference, that of aid to the front-line states in Southern Africa, would not be an occasion for deemphasizing the need for tough economic action in the form of sanctions against South Africa. There had been some talk that this might become a substitute for or an alternative to sanctions. That is probably the case as far as Great Britain was concerned. As the conference unfolded, it became clear that Britain was willing to consider this whole matter of aid to the front-line states in a way that it was not willing to consider the question of sanctions.
Fortunately, it appears that all the other Commonwealth leaders did not see this suggestion of increased aid to the frontline states as an alternative to or a substitute for economic sanctions against South Africa. Some of the worry that I had at the time I raised the question has since been alleviated by the conference itself.
This might be an opportunity to say a word or two of appreciation for the obvious sincerity with which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) holds his views of opposition to apartheid in South Africa. On this side of the House, we were

October 19, 1987
Adjournment Debate
all glad to see that the Prime Minister was generally recognized to have shown leadership on this issue, and generally recognized to have held his ground and the common ground of all the other nations of the Commonwealth, except Britain, with respect to the need for preserving those sanctions that are already there, and with respect to accelerating both the substance and the effect of sanctions.
We look forward to Canadian action on that. We not only hope but feel that the Prime Minister, in order to preserve and enhance that perception of integrity on this issue which he came out of that conference with, in a very short period of time will need to indicate what else Canada is prepared to do in order to make good the rhetoric of the Prime Minister.
It is certainly an occasion to notice that the Prime Minister in common with other leaders, resisted the obvious desire of Prime Minister Thatcher of Great Britain to roll back the sanction agenda and to change the focus of the Commonwealth in respect of South Africa.
It is always easier to show independence when it comes to a former colonial master, and we congratulate the Prime Minister on the extent to which he demonstrated that kind of independence of Great Britain. However, we have been independent of Great Britain for a long time now. Where we need to show an equal measure of independence in our foreign policy is the whole matter of Central America and our relationship with the United States, our current colonial master when it comes to foreign policy.
I hope that the same spirit of independence which imbued the Prime Minister on the occasion of the conference in Vancouver will soon imbue the Government in respect of its attitude toward Central America. I hope, in the same way as we have a Canadian Government ready to speak out independently against apartheid in South Africa, regardless of what Great Britain might think, and to advocate policies which are at odds with what Great Britain might think, that some day we will have a Government which is willing to advocate policies in Central America which are at odds with what the United States might think, a Government free to speak up against continuing American aid to the Contras, a Government willing to locate an embassy in Managua, and a Government willing to increase rather than decrease its aid to Nicaragua.
Canada could be doing a variety of other things which I argue today would be consistent with the spirit of independence in foreign policy areas that the Prime Minister displayed in Vancouver vis-a-vis Great Britain. We would like to see that same kind of independence displayed vis-a-vis the United States, particularly in respect of Central America and also in respect of other issues. We look forward to the day when the independent foreign policy perspective which the Prime Minister displayed in Vancouver will be comprehensive.

Madam Speaker, I must thank my colleague for referring to our Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) spirit of independence. In my estimation, if in recent months there was a country which showed openmindedness in all the conferences in which we as a country took part... On behalf of the Prime Minister, I am proud to accept this compliment from my colleague.

In that specific case the Government's commitment to assisting the FLS economies is well known. In total, Canada provides about $140 million in development co-operation to southern Africa annually.
The principal channel through which Canadian development assistance is provided to the FLS is the Southern African Development Co-ordination Conference, a regional organization of nine southern African states committed to accelerated economic development and reduced dependence on South Africa through increased regional integration and selfreliance. Canada has been one of SADCC's main supporters with annual disbursements of between $25 million and $30 million. These figures will, if anything, be increased over the next five years.
In addition, Canada provides assistance to individual frontline states through multilateral-food aid and humanitarian assistance-and NGO channels, as well as through the bilateral and specialized divisions of CIDA.

The issue of assistance to the front-line states, which we are debating, received attention most recently at the meeting of Commonwealth Heads of Government just concluded in Vancouver. Canada played a prominent role in developing an enhanced Commonwealth program to complement the work of other agencies in the region. Commonwealth leaders agreed to a statement and program of action which commits them, inter alia, to give priority attention to the rehabilitation and protection of the Limpopo railway line and the port of Maputo, to examine transit rights of the landlocked FLS of the region and to establish a special fund for technical assistance to Mozambique. They also announced their readiness to consult with a view to enabling those members in a position to do so, to make appropriate contributions to the security needs of Mozambique and other FLS requiring help.
For our part we have already made known our commitment to contribute $20 million towards the rehabilitation of the Limpopo railway line. We are in the process of examining ways in which Canadian support for the other elements of the Commonwealth statement and plan of action can best be implemented.
We do not consider assistance to the neighbouring countries as a substitute for firm economic action against South Africa. The Okanagan Statement issued on October 16 makes it clear that all members of the Commonwealth, except one, believe
